chapters.title: Conventions and Terminology
chapters.html:
Terminology. The following conventions are used consistently throughout the monograph. Archetype denotes a unit of typological classification within the Dar system (81 archetypes in total). Dar is, in the authorial terminology of the model, a synonym for archetype; in the academic chapters (1–4 and 8–10) the term archetype is preferred, while in the systematic chapters (5–7), which set out the content of the model itself, the authorial term Dar is employed. Field denotes one of the nine archetypal groups coded by the digits 1 through 9. Triadic code (or simply code) denotes the individual characterisation of a person within the system, having the form Ma–Zhi–Kun.

Notation of codes. The triadic code is written with hyphens: 1-6-7 means Ma = 1, Zhi = 6, Kun = 7. When reference is made to the position of an individual digit within the code, the designations Ma-digit, Zhi-digit, Kun-digit are used, or the corresponding positional designations of the first, second, and third place.

Bibliographic references. The in-text format [Author, year] is used, with the full list provided at the end of each chapter. On the first mention of a non-Russian author, the original Latin spelling of the name is given; thereafter the same spelling is retained throughout the English-language edition. Page references to directly quoted passages are given in square brackets after the year: [Author, year, p. NN].

Address to the reader. The monograph employs principally the impersonal academic style (“it is considered”, “it is shown”, “it is discussed”). In passages where the authors express their personal position or invite the reader to their own reflection, the form we (referring to the collective of authors) or the neutral the reader is used.

Digital resources. All digital resources mentioned in the monograph — the YupDar application, the research platform nauka-yupdar.vercel.app, and the Open Science Framework archive — are operational at the time of manuscript preparation. The authors maintain these resources in working order and undertake to preserve access to them for the extended period required for the reproducibility and verification of the empirical data.

Technically, the monograph has been prepared in accordance with the requirements of the Higher Attestation Commission (VAK) of the Russian Federation for scholarly publications, ensuring its eligibility for formal entry into the scholarly record and citation.

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
This monograph offers a systematic exposition of the authorial typological model Dars — an original system of 81 archetypal patterns derived deterministically from biographical parameters. The work applies the Kantian distinction between noumenon and phenomenon to the analysis of the YupLand digital ecosystem, in which the typological model serves as the architectural core.

The monograph develops in sequence:

the philosophical and methodological framework of the noumenon/phenomenon distinction as applied to digital typological artifacts;

the theoretical foundations of the Dar model (the Ma–Zhi–Kun triadic structure, the nine archetypal fields, and the 81 archetypes divided into three classes);

the algorithm for generating an individual profile;

a systematic exposition of the three classes of archetypes (64 basic, 16 integral, 1 special);

the architecture of the YupLand digital ecosystem as an artifact of the embodiment of the noumenal structure — including its proprietary cryptocurrency DarAi and the Principle of Dar-Giving as the organisational foundation of the ecosystem;

an empirical study of the phenomenon of user self-recognition in a personal archetype.

The structure of the monograph is built on a spiral logic. First, the methodological framework is established (Introduction; Chapter 1; Chapter 2: The Philosophical and Methodological Framework). Next, the theoretical structure of the model is unfolded (Chapter 3) and its operating algorithm is described (Chapter 4). The 81 archetypes are then set out systematically across their three classes (Chapters 5–7). The digital ecosystem is presented as an object of embodiment (Chapter 8); the empirical study is reported (Chapter 9); and limitations and prospects are discussed (Chapter 10).

The work is addressed to psychologists, psychiatrists, philosophers, developers of digital products, and researchers of metaverses, as well as to the wider readership interested in contemporary personality typology and the philosophy of digital identity.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The General Outline of the Work and the Justification of the Methodological Choice
chapters.html:
1.1. The Digitalisation of Self-Description and Self-Identification: A New Class of Artifacts

The first quarter of the twenty-first century has placed humankind in a cultural condition for which history offers no exact analogue. The greater part of everyday life now unfolds in digital environments: social networks, messaging applications, games, educational platforms, work applications. Within these environments the user does more than consume information; he or she actively constructs an identity, creating profiles, choosing avatars, taking typological tests, receiving “archetypes,” “types,” “classes,” “signs,” “levels.” The algorithms of recommender systems, in their turn, generate invisible typological profiles of users, on the basis of which all subsequent interaction is constructed [Cheney-Lippold, 2011; Striphas, 2015].

Digital self-description has become a mass-scale practice. On social-network platforms in the 2020s, the mini-formats of typologising tests gained widespread circulation (from MBTI applications to “brand archetypes”), alongside numerous popular typologies frequently lacking scientific validation. In parallel, a new class of digital products is taking shape, in which the typological model functions not as an auxiliary tool but as the architectural core of the entire ecosystem. Such products include multiplayer role-playing games with their systems of character classes [Yee, 2014], platforms for the gamification of learning [Hamari et al., 2014], corporate HR systems built on MBTI and the Big Five, and ecosystems of self-cognition and mental wellness increasingly organised around authorial typologies.

These phenomena, for all their heterogeneity, constitute a common class, which we propose to designate digital typological artifacts. They share several structural features:

the presence of an explicit classification system (types, archetypes, classes, levels);

an algorithm for assigning the user to one of the elements of the system;

a personalised presentation of the result (text, image, profile);

the integration of the typological profile with other elements of the digital environment (gamification, communities, recommendations);

a sustained feedback loop from the user in the form of identification, refusal, emotional reaction, or behavioural change.

Despite the mass-scale dissemination of these artifacts, systematic philosophical and psychological inquiry into their nature remains scarce. The research literature has addressed particular aspects, such as the psychometric validity of specific typologies [Briggs Myers et al., 1998; Costa & McCrae, 1992] or the social effects of online games [Yee, 2014], yet it does not encompass the class of typological artifacts as a whole, and offers no general methodology for their study.

We propose here a step towards such a methodology. The monograph is written on the material of one concrete digital typological artifact: the YupLand ecosystem with its authorial typological model Dars. The methodological approach advanced in the work is nonetheless applicable, in principle, to any typologically organised digital environment.

1.2. The Problem: What Is It That We Study When We Study Digital Typology

When the researcher approaches the study of a typological artifact within a digital environment, he or she is immediately confronted with a fundamental methodological difficulty: what, exactly, is the object of the investigation?

Three distinct answers are possible.

1. The typology as such. The researcher studies the classification system as an objective characteristic of reality. He or she asks: “Do sixteen personality types really exist? Is the world really divided into sixty-four archetypes? Do the five factors of the Big Five really exhaust the structure of personality?” This question leads in the direction of metaphysics and possesses no reliable empirical methods of resolution. No quantity of behavioural observations can answer definitively whether the “personality type” exists as a real entity or merely as a convenient mode of grouping.

2. The user’s reception of the typology. Here the researcher studies how users react to the classification: whether they recognise themselves in it, whether they consider the description accurate, whether they accept it. This approach addresses the phenomenological experience of the person, and at once invites several suspicions. Does it not reduce, in the end, to the Barnum effect [Forer, 1949] — the phenomenon of accepting any vague description presented as personal?

3. The artifact in its entirety. The researcher studies neither the typology as structure nor the user’s reaction in isolation, but the interaction between the classification system and the user under the conditions of a digital environment. This object is more complex, yet it corresponds most adequately to the nature of the digital typological artifact.

The third answer demands a methodology capable of working with a twofold object: the typology is at once a structure (the classification declared by the author) and a phenomenon (the observable user response). These two levels cannot be conflated, yet neither can they be definitively separated, for the artifact exists precisely as their unity.

For working with such a duality, the European philosophical tradition offers a fitting conceptual instrument: the Kantian distinction between noumenon and phenomenon. The following section is devoted to this distinction.

1.3. The Methodological Choice: Noumenon or Phenomenon

In the Critique of Pure Reason, Immanuel Kant introduced a systematic distinction between the phenomenon (the thing as it appears to us in experience) and the noumenon (the thing in itself, Ding an sich), which exists independently of our perception and is grasped only by reason, never observed directly [Kant, 1781]. This pair of concepts has become one of the load-bearing constructions of all subsequent European philosophy of mind, and it laid the foundation for the phenomenological tradition of Edmund Husserl [Husserl, 1913].

Applied to our task, this distinction proves remarkably apposite. The authorial typological model Dars, like any theoretical classification system, exists on two levels.

At the noumenal level, it is the structure the author sets out in The Book of DARs: a system of 81 archetypes computed by a deterministic algorithm from the user’s biographical parameters. This structure is declared as an objective characteristic of reality, in the sense that it exists independently of whether any particular person is aware of it. At the noumenal level the typology is not accessible to immediate perception. It can only be thought, by grasping its internal logic and principles of construction.

At the phenomenal level, it is the totality of manifestations observable in the experience of the user of the digital ecosystem. When the person enters a date of birth, sees a three-position code, reads the personal description of the archetype, recognises or fails to recognise himself or herself in it, returns to the product, or shares the result with those close to him or her, all of this constitutes phenomena accessible to empirical observation. They can be measured, compared, described.

The methodological choice of the present monograph consists in working with the phenomenal level, while declaring the noumenal level as a theoretical framework without laying claim to its empirical verification.

This choice carries a fundamental significance. It absolves the monograph of the false task of “proving that the Dar system works,” a task frequently demanded of typological systems and one that, in a strict empirical sense, is unresolvable for any typology (neither for the Big Five, nor for MBTI, nor for the Enneagram). Instead, we address a different scholarly task: we describe how the declared noumenal structure manifests itself in the observable phenomena of the digital environment.

An analogous methodological resolution is employed in contemporary philosophy of mind in discussions of the problem of qualia [Chalmers, 1996], in social phenomenology in the study of collective representations [Schutz, 1967], and in narrative psychology in the work with autobiographical texts. In every such case the researcher sets aside metaphysical claims about the object’s nature, and attends instead to how it is given to consciousness.

Phenomenological methodology has long been recognised for its scholarly fruitfulness. Its application to new objects, the digital typological artifacts, represents a natural development of the tradition under new historical conditions.

1.4. The Aims and Objectives of the Monograph

We can now formulate the principal aim of this monograph, together with a series of specific objectives.

Aim. On the material of the authorial typological model Dars and the YupLand digital ecosystem, to develop and demonstrate a methodological approach to the study of digital typological artifacts, grounded in the distinction between the noumenal and phenomenal levels of analysis.

Objective 1. To make explicit the philosophical and methodological framework of the work; to justify the application of the noumenon/phenomenon distinction to the class of digital typological artifacts; to examine its connections with contemporary digital anthropology, the theory of algorithmic identity, and the problem of the Barnum effect.

Objective 2. To set out systematically the theoretical foundations of the authorial typological model Dars — the triadic Ma–Zhi–Kun code structure, the system of nine archetypal fields, the classification of archetypes into three classes (64 basic, 16 integral, 1 special), and their mathematical completeness.

Objective 3. To describe the algorithm for generating an individual profile — the deterministic procedure for computing the triadic code from the date of birth, the multi-level architecture of the model, and the properties of the algorithm with respect to its reproducibility and verifiability.

Objective 4. To set out systematically the 81 archetypes that constitute the full substantive content of the model, distinguishing the three classes and employing a uniform structure of description for each archetype.

Objective 5. To describe the architecture of the YupLand digital ecosystem as an artifact of the embodiment of the noumenal structure — including its gamification, educational, and social functions, and the mode of integration of the typology into the digital environment.

Objective 6. To carry out an empirical examination of the basic hypotheses concerning the phenomenon of user self-recognition in the personal archetype, on a pilot online sample and with the use of standard psychometric methods.

Objective 7. To formulate prospects for further research; to indicate open questions, methodological limitations, and a programme of future publications on the topic.

The completion of the objectives enumerated above yields an integrated picture of one digital typological artifact and, at the same time, a methodological model applicable to a wider range of analogous objects.

The work opens a new field of inquiry: the study of how algorithmically mediated typological descriptions are incorporated into the self-perception of the person. In a clinical context, this is especially pertinent for patients with anxiety, depressive, and borderline disorders, for whom the search for a stable language of self-description may play both a supportive and a pathogenic role.

The monograph offers an example of the application of the classical European philosophical tradition to new objects of research. The Kantian distinction between noumenon and phenomenon, when applied to digital typological artifacts, opens the prospect of a renewal of phenomenological methodology under the conditions of the twenty-first century. It provides a basis for reflection on the use of typological systems in design — particularly in the field of mental-wellness applications, educational platforms, and gaming products — and proposes criteria for the conditions under which typological personalisation becomes an instrument of user self-cognition rather than merely a retention metric.

The investigation is conducted on the example of a metaverse: the profile of the user’s digital personal identity is examined, and the monograph offers a case study of one concrete small-scale ecosystem in which the typological structure organises a substantial part of the user experience. The analysis of this case may contribute to a general understanding of how digital identity is formed under conditions of algorithmic mediation. The work presents a structured exposition of the authorial typological system, which may be employed in individual psychological work with people as one instrument of reflection and self-understanding, and may also be applied to the analysis of group dynamic environments, both gamified and social.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Philosophical and Methodological Framework
chapters.html:
2.1. The Kantian Distinction between Noumenon and Phenomenon

In the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), the watershed work for all subsequent European philosophy, Immanuel Kant drew one of the most consequential distinctions in the history of philosophical thought — the distinction between phenomenon and noumenon [Kant, 1781].

The phenomenon in Kant is the thing as it appears to us (Greek φαινόμενον, “that which appears”). It is all that is accessible to us through the forms of sensible intuition (space and time) and the categories of the understanding (quantity, quality, relation, modality). Phenomena constitute the world of experience: observable, measurable, amenable to scientific study. When we see the trunk of a tree, feel the warmth of a hand, or hear the sound of a bell, we are dealing with phenomena.

The noumenon is the thing in itself, the Ding an sich (Greek νοούμενον, “that which is grasped by mind”). It is what exists independently of our perception and is apprehended by reason alone, never by the organs of sense. Noumena constitute the intelligible plane of reality: they are inaccessible to direct observation, yet may be thought as conditions and grounds of phenomenal experience. Kant insisted repeatedly that the noumenon cannot be known in the strict sense; it can only be thought, as the boundary of cognition itself [Kant, 1781, A 235–260 / B 294–315].

This distinction was not Kant’s invention ex nihilo. It has long roots in the European philosophical tradition. Plato, in the Republic and the Timaeus, drew a distinction between the world of Ideas (intelligible essences) and the world of appearances (imperfect copies of the Ideas in matter) [Plato, Republic; Timaeus]. Aristotle, in the Metaphysics, elaborated the conception of form and matter, in which form figures as the intelligible principle of the thing. Mediaeval Scholasticism developed the doctrine of the distinction between essence (essentia) and existence (existentia) [Aquinas, 1265–1274]. Kant synthesised this long tradition and gave it a rigorous form responsive to the demands of early modern science.

Kant’s distinction breaks new ground precisely in its methodological consequences. He did not merely state the twofoldness of the world; he drew from it a practical lesson for scientific cognition. Empirical science works with phenomena. Metaphysical assertions about noumena, strictly speaking, exceed the bounds of scientific method and belong to the domain of speculative thought.

The Kantian distinction received substantial development in the phenomenological tradition founded by Edmund Husserl in the first third of the twentieth century [Husserl, 1913]. Husserl proposed that the phenomenon be regarded not as “the appearance of something hidden behind it,” but as an autonomous reality of consciousness disclosed in acts of perception. The phenomenological method requires of the researcher a temporary abstention (Greek ἐποχή, epoché) from metaphysical assertions about the nature of the object under study, and a concentration on how this object is given to consciousness. This method — phenomenological reduction — has become one of the most fruitful instruments in the humanities of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. It is applied in narrative psychology in the analysis of autobiographical accounts [Bruner, 1990], in sociology in the study of the everyday [Schutz, 1967], in the anthropology of religion in the analysis of sacred experiences [Eliade, 1957], and in contemporary philosophy of mind in discussions of the problem of qualia [Chalmers, 1996].

The common denominator of all these applications is a single methodological stance: the researcher does not attempt to “prove” or “refute” the ontological status of the object under study, but concentrates on the phenomenology of this object — on how it is experienced, how it functions in experience, how it shapes behaviour. This stance liberates the research process from false tasks and permits concentration on productive questions.

In the twenty-first century, the Kantian distinction acquires a new pertinence in connection with the appearance of a new class of objects of inquiry: algorithmically mediated cultural artifacts. Profiles on social networks, recommender systems, typological tests, digital archetypes, virtual identities — all these phenomena yield only with difficulty to classical empirical investigation, for they are at once structures (mathematically specified systems) and phenomena (objects experienced by users).

Contemporary digital anthropology, as developed in the work of J. Cheney-Lippold, T. Striphas, and N. Brügger, attends to this class of objects and proposes that they be regarded as hybrid ontological forms [Cheney-Lippold, 2011; Striphas, 2015; Brügger, 2018]. Cheney-Lippold introduces the concept of algorithmic identity — a form of self-description in which the person receives his or her social and psychological characterisation not through introspection or expert diagnosis, but through algorithmic assignment on the basis of biographical, behavioural, or other data.

Algorithmic identities possess a paradoxical nature: on the one hand, they are formed by strict mathematical rules and therefore bear the marks of structure; on the other, they are experienced by the user as a living characterisation of the self and are therefore phenomena. The Kantian distinction permits these two levels to be discriminated and worked with separately, without conflation.

It is precisely this methodological possibility that we employ in the present monograph in the analysis of the YupLand digital ecosystem and the authorial typological model Dars.

2.2. Phenomenological Reduction as a Method for Working with Twofold Objects

The structure of phenomenological reduction. Phenomenological reduction, as developed by Edmund Husserl, constitutes a rigorous methodological procedure composed of several successive steps [Husserl, 1913, §§ 31–32]. The first step is the epoché, or abstention from the natural attitude. The researcher consciously “switches off” the supposition that the object under study exists in the ordinary empirical sense. He or she neither affirms nor denies the reality of the object, but simply refrains from employing this supposition as a working hypothesis. The second step is phenomenological reduction in the proper sense. The researcher turns attention to the very act of consciousness in which the object is given. Not “what the object is in itself,” but “how the object is presented to consciousness” becomes the matter of analysis. The third step is eidetic reduction. The researcher varies the representations of the object in imagination, attempting to identify its essential characteristics — those features without which the object ceases to be itself. This procedure permits a structural description of the object to be obtained without departing from the phenomenological attitude.

Applying this three-step procedure to our object of inquiry (the authorial Dar model as realised in the YupLand digital ecosystem), we obtain the following. Epoché: we consciously abstain from assertions about the metaphysical nature of the Dar model. We neither affirm nor deny that the 81 archetypes “really exist” as an objective characteristic of the human personality. This question we set aside, outside the bounds of the present work. Phenomenological reduction: we concentrate on how the Dar model is given to the user’s consciousness under the conditions of the digital ecosystem. When the user enters a date of birth, sees the triadic code, reads the personal description of the archetype, recognises or fails to recognise himself or herself in it, or proceeds into the product for the full deciphering — all these phenomena become the matter of our analysis. Eidetic reduction: we attempt to isolate the essential characteristics of the phenomenon of user self-recognition in the personal archetype — those features that make this phenomenon precisely what it is. At this level we formulate a working model of four mechanisms by which the noumenal structure is embodied in phenomenal experience (for the detailed account, see Chapter 3).

The application of phenomenological reduction to the study of digital typological artifacts yields several important epistemological advantages.

Liberation from the false task of proof. Typological systems have historically often become the subject of a falsely posed question: “Do these types really exist?” This question, for all its apparent meaningfulness, lends itself poorly to scientific resolution. No quantity of empirical observations can definitively settle whether the “personality type” exists as a real entity or merely as a convenient mode of grouping. Phenomenological reduction reformulates the task: instead of demonstrating existence, we study functioning — how the typological structure works in the user’s experience.

The preservation of substantive rigour. Abstention from metaphysical assertions does not amount to a renunciation of rigour. Phenomenological description is subject to its own criteria of correctness: it must be exhaustive (taking into account all essential aspects of the object’s givenness), differentiated (distinguishing different modes of givenness), and reproducible (another researcher, applying the same procedure, must obtain comparable results). This is its own scholarly rigour — distinct from that of the natural-scientific experiment, but no less demanding.

The expansion of the field of observation. The phenomenological attitude permits the inclusion within the field of observation of aspects of experience that often remain beyond the bounds of classical quantitative research: the user’s emotional response, the sense of “fit” or “miss,” the process of reflection upon one’s own archetype, the change of self-description after receipt of the profile. In quantitative research these aspects ordinarily remain “noise”; in the phenomenological approach they become part of the principal material.

Mixed-methods as the contemporary realisation of the phenomenological approach. In contemporary empirical psychology, the phenomenological approach is most often realised through mixed-methods design — a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods within a single study [Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018]. Quantitative data (scales, scores, statistical indices) provide breadth of coverage and the testability of hypotheses. Qualitative data (free-text responses, thematic analysis, narrative analysis) provide depth of understanding and phenomenological fullness.

The empirical study described in Chapter 9 of the present monograph employs precisely this mixed strategy. In addition to quantitative scales of self-recognition, respondents provide free-text answers in an open-question format, which are subjected to qualitative thematic analysis. This makes it possible to obtain at once a testable statistic and a phenomenologically rich description of the user’s experience.

2.3. Contemporary Digital Anthropology and Algorithmic Identity

2.3.1. The Concept of Algorithmic Identity

Contemporary digital anthropology, intensively developed over the last two decades, has introduced a number of concepts essential for understanding new forms of self-description. The central one is the concept of algorithmic identity, elaborated in the work of J. Cheney-Lippold [Cheney-Lippold, 2011; 2017].

Algorithmic identity is a form of social and psychological self-description in which the characterisation of the person is formed not through classical channels (self-report, expert diagnosis, social attribution), but through algorithmic assignment on the basis of some body of data about him or her. These data may be behavioural (history of clicks, duration of sessions, patterns of interaction), biographical (date of birth, place of residence, education), social (network connections, group affiliations), or physiological (biometrics, vocal characteristics).

The algorithm assigns the person to one of a set of pre-given categories, and this category begins to shape his or her further experience: recommendations, content, offers, assessments, access. Gradually the person becomes what the algorithm has defined him or her to be — not because the algorithm has discovered his or her “true nature,” but because the environment around the person is now shaped to fit the category the algorithm has issued.

This process Cheney-Lippold names soft biopolitics — a form of population management by means of algorithmic categorisation, requiring neither open power nor coercion, acting through the shaping of self-perception.

2.3.2. Algorithmic Culture

T. Striphas introduces a broader concept: algorithmic culture [Striphas, 2015]. By this is understood a condition in which basic cultural categories — taste, identity, belonging, value — are formed under the substantial influence of algorithmic systems. Striphas observes that algorithms have ceased to be mere instruments of data processing; they have become cultural agents, shaping the very landscape of meanings within which the contemporary person lives.

In algorithmic culture, the very concept of self-cognition is transformed. Whereas in traditional culture the person recognised himself or herself through comparison with sacred texts, mythological archetypes, philosophical teachings, or expert diagnoses, in algorithmic culture he or she recognises the self through algorithmically issued categories — whether brand archetypes, psychological types, horoscopic signs, or character classes in games. These categories function as a new language of self-description.

2.3.3. Digital Typological Artifacts as a Class

If the observations of digital anthropology are generalised, a distinct class of cultural artifacts may be identified: digital typological artifacts. They are united by the following features:

Structural typological organisation. The artifact contains an explicit classification system (types, archetypes, classes, levels, signs) that constitutes its semantic core.

Algorithmic assignment of the user. A procedure exists which, on the basis of definite input parameters of the user, assigns him or her to one of the categories of the system.

Personalised presentation of the result. The category is presented to the user in the form of a personal profile — text, image, narrative.

Integration with other elements of the digital environment. The typological profile is linked to the rest of the ecosystem: to recommendations, gamification, social functions, and economy.

The phenomenological effect of self-recognition. The user responds to his or her profile not as an external instrument but as something pertaining to the self; this experience becomes part of the person’s self-description.

These features are met by phenomena that may at first appear heterogeneous: character classes in role-playing online games, MBTI applications, corporate typological services, ecosystems such as YupLand, horoscope services on social networks, brand archetypes in marketing. Despite the differences of their concrete realisations, all of them form a single class of artifacts, sharing common methodological problems of study.

2.3.4. The Place of the Dar Model within This Class

The authorial typological model Dars, as realised within the YupLand ecosystem, occupies a particular position within the class of digital typological artifacts, owing to several characteristics.

The determinacy of the algorithm. Unlike recommender systems (where the category is formed on the basis of behavioural signals and is therefore potentially variable), and unlike questionnaire-based typologies (where the category depends on the user’s self-report at a given moment), in the Dar model the category is fully determined by biographical parameters (the date of birth) and does not change over time. This affords a high degree of formal transparency in the procedure.

The multi-layered character of the description. Unlike simple typologies (for example, the division of people into the four temperaments), the Dar model contains a triadic structure of three positions (Ma, Zhi, Kun), three classes of archetypes (basic, integral, special), and a six-block description of each archetype. This affords a high substantive density.

Integration with its own economy. The YupLand ecosystem includes its own cryptocurrency, DarAi, and is organised on the Principle of Dar-Giving, which creates an additional social context around the typological profile.

Openness to empirical investigation. The authors of the system have purposefully created a research platform (nauka-yupdar.vercel.app) on which the collection of anonymised data for scholarly analysis is carried out. This is a phenomenon rare in the industry of digital typologies.

The conjunction of these characteristics renders the Dar model a fitting object of inquiry for the elaboration of a general methodology for the analysis of digital typological artifacts.

2.4. The Application of the Methodological Framework to the Authorial Typological System Dars

In accordance with the methodological framework adopted, we regard the Dar model as a noumenal construct. This means the following.

The model is declared by its authors (Ya. S. Sibirskiy, as systematised by S. N. Nesterova) as an objective characteristic of reality — a typological structure of 81 archetypes computed deterministically from biographical parameters of the user. This structure is posited as existing as a condition of the personality, irrespective of whether the person is himself or herself aware of it.

The positing of such a structure is the typical step of any typological theory. Analogous postulates are adopted by the authors of MBTI (sixteen types as objective configurations of the psyche), of the Big Five (five factors as the fundamental axes of personality), of the Enneagram (nine types as structural strategies), of the Human Design system (sixteen profiles as biologically conditioned patterns). In each of these systems, the postulate of the existence of the typological structure is not empirically demonstrated; it is adopted as a theoretical foundation.

Our methodological relation to the Dar model is, therefore, in no way exceptional. We apply to it the same framework that is applied to all serious typological systems: we accept the structure as declared, without attempting either to prove or to refute it in its noumenal form.

What we study at the empirical level is the phenomena of the embodiment of the noumenal structure within the YupLand digital ecosystem. These include:

The phenomenon of algorithmic computation. When the user enters a date of birth, a digital algorithm produces a visible three-position code. This is a phenomenon objectively observable: it occurs in real time, it is reproducible, and it is identical for identical input data across different users.

The phenomenon of personalised presentation. On the basis of the code, a textual description of the archetype is generated. In our implementation, this description is created by the DeepSeek language model through an AI agent trained on annotated datasets, at the moment of the user’s request, which secures the uniqueness of each instance while preserving the common structure. The phenomenon of description generation is a measurable event.

The phenomenon of subjective recognition. Having read the description, the user evaluates its correspondence to his or her experience. This evaluation is recorded on a Likert scale and in free-text responses. The phenomenon of recognition is a psychological event measurable by standard methods.

The phenomenon of behavioural engagement. After completing the questionnaire, the user either proceeds into the principal application (YupDar) for the full deciphering, or does not. This is a behavioural event objectively registered by the server infrastructure.

The phenomenon of social exchange. Users share their archetypal profiles with those close to them, discuss them, compare them, and test them for compatibility. This is a phenomenon of social communication, registered through the metrics of use of the corresponding functions of the ecosystem.

The phenomenon of somatic resonance. In particular cases, directed work with the archetype is accompanied by measurable somatic effects — changes in body temperature, heart rate, or state of relaxation. This phenomenon is not the principal subject of the present monograph, but is indicated as a direction of further investigation requiring its own methodological elaboration.

Each of the phenomena enumerated is measurable. For each it is possible to collect data, to conduct statistical analysis, and to formulate and test hypotheses.

It is essential that our investigation studies neither the noumenon nor the phenomena in isolation, but the relation between them. The concrete research question is formulated thus:

“If the noumenal structure of the Dars is declared by the authors as existing, with what consistency and stability does it manifest itself in the observable phenomena of the digital environment?”

A positive answer to this question does not amount to a demonstration of the ontological existence of the Dars — that question lies beyond our methodology. A positive answer signifies only that the declared structure is phenomenologically consistent: it produces stable, reproducible, and differentiable phenomena in the user’s experience.

This is a research claim moderate in its pretensions but methodologically clean. It accords with the principles of contemporary academic work and is comparable in epistemological status with the majority of investigations in the psychology of typologies [Furnham, 2020].

2.5. The Barnum Effect and the Methodological Control of It

The classical description of the Barnum effect [Forer, 1949]. One of the principal challenges to any investigation of self-recognition in typological descriptions is the effect described by B. R. Forer in 1949 [Forer, 1949]. In the classical experiment, Forer distributed to a group of students “personal descriptions of the personality” — which were, in fact, a single universal text composed of stock statements of an astrological character. When the students were asked to assess the accuracy of the description on a 5-point scale, the mean score was 4.3 out of 5: the students, on the whole, accepted a universal text as personally fitted to them.

This phenomenon has come to be known as the Barnum effect, after the circus impresario Phineas Taylor Barnum, to whom the phrase “I have something for everybody” is attributed. The effect is also occasionally called the Forer effect or the effect of subjective validation.

The Barnum effect is a serious methodological obstacle for any typological system that employs textual descriptions. It demonstrates that a high score of recognition does not, by itself, prove the substantive validity of the typology: people are inclined to recognise themselves in any generalised description presented as personal.

In subsequent investigations [Furnham & Schofield, 1987; Forer, 1949 — and replications thereof], the conditions under which the Barnum effect is strengthened or weakened were identified.

Conditions of strengthening:

The description contains mixed statements (positive and neutral characterisations).

The description is presented as personalised — as derived from some data about the subject (date of birth, test answers, biometrics).

The source of the description is perceived as authoritative or technological (a psychologist, an algorithm, an AI).

The description corresponds to generally socially desirable traits (purposefulness, sensitivity, capacity for empathy).

Conditions of weakening:

The description contains specific statements not applicable to the majority of people.

The description contains negative characterisations (shadow features) that the person is not inclined to accept on his or her own account.

The experiment includes a control comparison: the subject is also shown a description for another person (or another typological category), and the difference in acceptance is measured.

Contemporary psychometric practice has developed several strategies for controlling the Barnum effect in the study of typological systems [Furnham, 2020].

Strategy 1. Control comparison with the opposite category. The user is shown the description not only of his or her own type but also of the type opposite to his or her own according to some mathematical or substantive criterion. If recognition of the user’s own type is significantly higher than recognition of the opposite, this constitutes an argument that the system operates not on the Barnum effect, but on substantive differentiation.

Strategy 2. Use of differentiated descriptions. Descriptions of different types are formulated so as to contain mutually incompatible statements. Were all descriptions to be generalised, the person would recognise himself or herself in any of them; when, however, the descriptions differ, recognition becomes more selective.

Strategy 3. Inclusion of specific and shadow statements. Specific particularities and negative characterisations are included in the description of the archetype. The acceptance of such statements on one’s own account is a stronger argument for substantive validity than the acceptance of universally positive statements.

Strategy 4. Correlation with independent external criteria. The results of the typology are compared with external measurements (behavioural, neurophysiological, observational). Coincidence with external criteria cannot be explained by the Barnum effect.

In our research, described in Chapter 9 of the present monograph, the first three strategies are employed. The control of the Barnum effect is realised as follows.

First, the control comparison. After reading the description of his or her own archetype, the respondent is shown the description of the diametrically opposite archetype, computed mathematically according to the rule of mirror fields: the position Ma is replaced by the opposite field, likewise Zhi, and Kun is recomputed. The respondent assesses recognition of this description on the same 7-point scale. Hypothesis H2 maintains that recognition of one’s own archetype is significantly higher than recognition of the opposite.

Second, the differentiation of descriptions. In our system, the descriptions of archetypes are generated by the DeepSeek language model with the use of specially designed prompts, large annotated data archives, and trained AI agents in the form of chatbots, which underscore the difference between archetypes. The description of the opposite archetype is structurally incompatible with the description of one’s own.

Third, the inclusion of specific and shadow statements. The description of each archetype in the Dar system contains, alongside the light side (describing the strengths), the active and passive shadows, describing compensatory patterns and the “deep fears” of the bearer of the archetype. These statements are frequently specific and negative, which lowers the risk of universal self-ascription.

The combined application of these three strategies provides a well-founded basis for the substantive interpretation of results. When the score of recognition of one’s own archetype significantly exceeds the score of recognition of the opposite — under the condition that differentiated and specific descriptions have been used — one may speak of the presence of a phenomenological effect not reducible to the Barnum effect.

2.6. The Correlation between the Small and the Large Social as a Philosophical and Methodological Possibility — the Phenomenological Window of Extrapolation through the Dar System

In addition to the basic methodology described above, the present work indicates an additional philosophical and methodological possibility, connected with the hypothesis of the correlation between the small and the large social. This hypothesis was formulated in the course of an experiment with AI agents trained on the basis of the algorithms of the Dar system, and was tested on two databases — of states and of multinational corporations; the results merit a separate methodological grounding.

The hypothesis is formulated as follows:

“If, within the small social (the community of users of the YupLand ecosystem), a stable distribution of typological archetypes and stable patterns of interaction among them are manifested, it may be supposed that within the large social (the general population, and other social communities not included in the investigation) analogous structures act, structures not accessible to direct observation on large samples without typological annotation.”

The hypothesis rests upon several methodological assumptions, which it is appropriate to make explicit.

Assumption 1. The distribution of archetypes by date of birth in the YupLand sample, given a sufficient sample size, approximates a uniform distribution across the calendar (since the algorithm uses only biographical parameters not dependent on product preferences).

Assumption 2. If the behavioural patterns of bearers of different archetypes within YupLand differ stably, these differences reflect typologically conditioned dispositions rather than the specifics of the YupLand audience.

Assumption 3. Behavioural dispositions manifesting themselves under the conditions of a digital environment manifest themselves, in one form or another, also in other social contexts, which permits the regularities observed in YupLand to be transferred to broader social communities.

Each of these assumptions is testable, given a sufficient volume of data. Taken together, they form a framework for the sociological extension of the work — a direction indicated in the programme of further research (see Chapter 10).

In terms of the phenomenological methodology we have adopted, the small social (the YupLand community) figures as a phenomenological window onto the large social. This concept requires experimental confirmation. By a phenomenological window is meant here a region of observation within which the researcher has direct access to phenomena of interest, while these phenomena are correlated with a substantially broader class of phenomena not directly observable. The microscope is a phenomenological window onto the world of cells. The medical record of the patient is a phenomenological window onto his or her integral psychophysical condition. An archive of literary manuscripts is a phenomenological window onto the creative life of a definite epoch.

A small community with typological annotation is a phenomenological window onto a large community without such annotation. The regularities observed in the small may, under definite methodological conditions, be extrapolated to the large. This operation of extrapolation is not a simple one; it requires a rigorous grounding of the correspondence between the small and the large. Yet the very possibility of such extrapolation renders the small community a methodologically valuable object of investigation.

The authors of the present monograph emphasise: the hypothesis is formulated as a research perspective, not as a ready-made instrument of social action. Any practical application of the Dar typology to large social groups requires a separate ethical grounding and experimental confirmation, and does not belong to the tasks of the present work. In Chapter 10 (Conclusion), this direction is indicated as one of the directions of future research requiring its own methodological and ethical elaboration.

In the present chapter, the philosophical and methodological framework upon which all subsequent work rests has been unfolded. The principal methodological positions adopted in the monograph are the following.

The authorial typological model Dars is regarded as a noumenal construct in the Kantian sense: a structure declared by its authors, existing as the theoretical foundation of the object of inquiry, but not subject to direct empirical verification. The YupLand digital ecosystem is regarded as the phenomenal embodiment of the noumenal structure.

The phenomena arising in the environment of the user’s interaction with the ecosystem — algorithmic computation, personalised presentation, subjective recognition, behavioural engagement, social exchange — constitute the subject of empirical investigation.

The method of research employed is phenomenological reduction, complemented by mixed-methods design. The epoché liberates us from the false task of demonstrating the ontology of the Dars; reduction and eidetic analysis permit the essential characteristics of the phenomena to be isolated. The Barnum effect is controlled by three strategies: control comparison with the opposite archetype, the differentiation of descriptions, and the inclusion of specific and shadow characterisations in the description. The additional research perspective — the hypothesis of the correlation between the small and the large social — is indicated as a direction of future work, lying beyond the bounds of the present monograph.

3.1. Triadic Ontology: Ma (Potential) — Zhi (Realisation) — Kun (Synthesis)

An introduction to the triadic structure. At the foundation of the authorial typological model Dars lies a triadic ontology — the conception that every stable pattern of personality may be described as the combination of three ontologically distinct levels. These levels are designated by the authorial terms Ma, Zhi, and Kun.

The triadic structure is not original to the Dar model. It belongs to a long typological and philosophical tradition in which the human being, or the world, is regarded through a threefold articulation. In philosophy, this is the triad being — existence — becoming (from Hegel to Heidegger). In psychology — the structural model of the psyche in S. Freud (Id — Ego — Superego), the functional triad of C. G. Jung (thinking — feeling — intuition/sensation), the level model of personality in A. F. Lazursky. In typology — the threefold articulation in the Enneagram (the instinctive, feeling, and thinking centres). In the Eastern traditions — the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) of Sāṃkhya philosophy, and the triad Jing — Qi — Shen of Daoist cosmology.

The authorial triad Ma — Zhi — Kun presents an autonomous conceptual formulation, not reducible directly to any of the traditions noted, yet drawing upon the same cognitive structure. It is appropriate to describe each of the three levels separately.

Ma — the inner potential. Ma is the first position of the triadic code, designating the level of the inner potential of the personality. It is the basic, root-level support from which the person draws his or her strength — the inner constant determining the character of response to situations at moments when external demands are absent or attenuated. It is the position of the first impression that the person produces upon others; the potential which may not yet be self-identified by its bearer, yet which is already apparent to the surrounding community. Briefly, it may be described as the unconscious behaviour of the person which others perceive and read. In the field of psychology, the position Ma corresponds to what contemporary personality psychology terms the dispositional core [McAdams, 1995] — the deep structure of stable dispositions forming the character. It is the level at which the personality “is itself in itself,” in relative independence of external observation. Phenomenologically, the position Ma is often described by bearers of archetypes as “what lies within,” “what I rest upon,” “when I am alone with myself.” Across different archetypes the content of this inner core differs: for some archetypes it is the need for structure and order; for others, the need for space and freedom; for others still, the need for connection with other people. Yet the level itself — the Ma position — is structurally identical for all 81 archetypes. In clinical psychiatry, an analogue of the Ma position may be sought in what K. Leonhard [Leonhard, 1968] termed the accentuated trait — a stable characterological feature manifesting, in especially acute forms, as accentuation. The position Ma is not pathological in itself; it represents the norm in the sense of a stable pattern. Yet it is precisely in the Ma position that both the resource-bearing and the compensatory sides of the archetype emerge most vividly.

Zhi — realisation in action. Zhi is the second position of the triadic code, designating the level of realisation in action, or the outer expression of potential. It is what in the person is accessible to direct observation: behaviour, style of communication, manner of decision-making, mode of interaction with circumstances. In psychology, the Zhi position corresponds to the behavioural stratum of personality — the level of habitual actions forming the recognisable outer contour of the person [Bandura, 1986]. It is the stratum at which the personality meets the world, and through which the world meets the personality. Phenomenologically, the Zhi position is described by bearers of archetypes through actions: “how I do,” “what is noticeable in me from outside,” “how I conduct myself at work or in relationships.” Across different archetypes the character of these actions differs. For some archetypes it is action through structure and system; for others, through empathy and connection; for others, through word and communication. Each such behavioural expression corresponds to a definite substantive directedness of the Zhi position.

The difference between Ma and Zhi may be described by the following metaphor: Ma is the roots of the tree (that upon which all rests, hidden from view); Zhi is the trunk and crown (the visible part, through which the tree interacts with the world). The metaphor conveys the principal relation: the inner foundation and the outer expression.

Kun — synthesis and the point of wholeness. Kun is the third position of the triadic code, designating the level of synthesis, or the point of integration of the inner potential and its outer expression. It is the zone of the personality in which Ma and Zhi meet and form a whole experience of the self.

In its psychological aspect, the Kun position approaches most closely what C. G. Jung termed the Self (Selbst) [Jung, 1959] — the integral centre of the personality, in which its various sides find harmonious co-existence. In Jung, the Self is an archetype towards which individuation strives (the process of becoming a whole personality). Yet within the Dar system the Kun position is not wholly identical with the Jungian Self: Kun is present in every archetype from the outset — not as an unattainable ideal, but as a structural element. Phenomenologically, the Kun position is described through the experience of connectedness, when the person feels that his or her actions, feelings, and self-understanding “compose themselves into a single whole.” In terms of self-perception, this experience finds expression in formulae such as “I know who I am,” “I have meaning,” “everything I do has a connection with everything else within me.”

A particular property of the Kun position is its mathematical determination: the third digit of the code is computed from the sum of the first two (see Chapter 4). This means that Kun is not an independent parameter of the personality, but constitutes a functional synthesis of the Ma and Zhi positions. This property reflects an important theoretical position of the model: the wholeness of the personality is not given independently, but arises from the interaction of its resource-bearing foundation and its outer expression.

Taken together, the three levels yield the model’s general theoretical claim:

Every stable pattern of personality is described by the triple Ma — Zhi — Kun, where Ma is the inner potential (the root-level support), Zhi is the outer expression (the behavioural contour), and Kun is the point of integration arising from the synthesis of the first two levels.

The triadic code, therefore, is no arbitrary classificatory scheme — it reflects the ontological structure of the personality as it is conceived by the author of the system. Each of the three positions has its own function:

Ma answers the question “out of what the person acts”;

Zhi answers the question “how the person acts”;

Kun answers the question “to what the person’s action leads.”

This triad is observable in different modalities. Ma is observed through introspection under conditions of relative repose (when external influences are minimised). Zhi is observed through the direct observation of behaviour. Kun is observed through the results of activity and through the experience of the connectedness of the personality itself.

3.2. The Nine Archetypal Fields

Each position of the triadic code (Ma, Zhi, or Kun) takes a value from 1 to 9. These nine values correspond to the nine archetypal fields. A field constitutes a stable functional-semantic characteristic determining the content of the corresponding level of the personality.

We use the expression archetypal field in a sense distinct from both the Jungian archetype and the physical field. Within the Dar system, a field is a basic category describing a definite modality of personal functioning. The nine fields form an exhaustive list of such modalities within the bounds of the present model.

The nine fields are systematised in the authorial work through a double support: substantively-functional (what each field represents as a principle) and naturally-elemental (correlation with the classical primary elements within a supplementary systematising structure). The double support furnishes the richness of substantive description of each field while simultaneously fixing it within a broader typological tradition. A summary characterisation of the nine fields is presented in Table 3.1.
