Each field is described more fully below.

Field 1. LOGOS. The principle of structure and foundation. The field of the organising beginning forming frames and hierarchies. In the personal aspect, it signifies the need for order, the habit of systematisation, the disposition to construct rules and regulations. In the cognitive aspect, it determines thinking through cause-and-effect relations. Within the archetypal tradition it stands closest to the Jungian archetype of the Wise Old Man in his aspect of Law.

Field 2. NIMA. The principle of spaciousness and capacity. The field in which diverse possibilities co-exist without being reduced to one. In the personal aspect, it signifies comfort in indeterminacy, the capacity to hold in mind several mutually incompatible perspectives, readiness for multiplicity. In the cognitive aspect, it determines thinking through possibilities and potentials. Within the tradition it stands close to the Jungian notion of active imagination, and to the Daoist category of wu wei (action through non-action).

Field 3. ANDRA. The principle of connection and union. The field of empathy, of the capacity to establish and sustain relationships. In the personal aspect, it is identified by sensitivity to the emotional ground of those around, the natural role of the connector, the inclination to process-oriented work with relationships. In the cognitive aspect, it determines thinking through emotional and relational structures. Within the tradition it is bound to the Jungian archetype of the Anima in her aspect of warmth and connection.

Field 4. ZINGRA. The principle of growth and transformation. The field of continuous evolution, of the search for new levels, of the passage from one form to another. In the personal aspect, it signifies an inner need for development, dissatisfaction with stagnation, readiness for radical change. In the cognitive aspect, it determines thinking through stages and transitions. Within the tradition it stands close to the archetype of the Hero in his aspect of transformation.

Field 5. LUBA. The principle of centre and will. The field of gathering around an inner axis, of the capacity to hold focus, to bring forth the volitional beginning. In the personal aspect, it manifests as a stable reliance upon “I am,” independence of external evaluation, the natural role of the assembly point. In the cognitive aspect, it determines thinking through priorities and hierarchies of goals. Within the tradition it stands close to the archetype of the King or the Ruler in his inner aspect.

Field 6. TUMA. The principle of movement and rhythm. The field of dynamics, the flow of time, the sense of the moment and of tempo. In the personal aspect — the inner chronotope, the feeling of “the right moment,” the capacity to synchronise with the tempo of circumstance. In the cognitive aspect, it determines thinking through sequences and cycles. Within the tradition it stands close to the Daoist Dao in its aspect of fluidity, and to the Jungian function of intuition.

Field 7. ASTRA. The principle of word and connection. The field of communication, of the transmission of meaning between people and systems. In the personal aspect, it establishes the natural role of mediator and transmitter, sensitivity to the word, the capacity to find a common language. In the cognitive aspect, it determines thinking through expressive structures and networks. Within the tradition it is bound to the archetype of Hermes/Mercury as the mediator between worlds.

Field 8. BITRA. The principle of boundaries and form. The field of holding, of protection, of giving form to potential within completed structures. In the personal aspect — the capacity to say “no,” to defend one’s own space, to bring what has been begun to a completed form. In the cognitive aspect, it determines thinking through perimeters and envelopes. Within the tradition it stands close to the archetype of the Guardian or the Keeper.

Field 9. OMA. The principle of wholeness and unity. The field of integrative perception, in which discrete elements compose a meaningful system. In the personal aspect — the capacity to see the picture as a whole, to preserve the connection among the heterogeneous aspects of life, to experience meaning. In the cognitive aspect, it determines thinking through holistic structures. Within the tradition it stands close to the Jungian Self and to the Kabbalistic notion of Ein Sof (the Infinite Whole).

3.2.1. Double Polarity: Inner and Outer Elements

A particular property of the system of nine fields is their paired organisation by the principle of double polarity. Fields 1–4, in the elemental systematisation, are correlated with the inner manifestations of the four classical elements (earth, air, water, fire). Fields 5–8 are correlated with the outer manifestations of the same four elements, but in the reverse order. The ninth field, OMA, is represented by ether, a category distinct from the four principal elements.

This twofold principle gives rise to the following pairs:

Inner element

Outer element

1. LOGOS (inner Earth)

8. BITRA (outer Earth)

2. NIMA (inner Air)

7. ASTRA (outer Air)

3. ANDRA (inner Water)

6. TUMA (outer Water)

4. ZINGRA (inner Fire)

5. LUBA (outer Fire)

Each pair is united by a common element yet distinguished by polarity. For instance, LOGOS and BITRA are both bound to the element of earth, but LOGOS operates at the level of inner structures (rules, foundation, cause-and-effect relations), while BITRA operates at the level of outer forms (boundaries, envelopes, protection). The same holds for the other pairs.

This paired organisation carries an important substantive significance: it establishes mirror relations between the fields, lying at the foundation of the mathematics of the computation of the opposite archetype (see Chapter 4, § 4.4) and employed in the empirical investigation for the control of the Barnum effect (see Chapter 2, § 2.5).

OMA, occupying a position outside the paired organisation, possesses a particular ontological status. The etheric field represents the level of integration of all the other fields; it is not opposed to any one of them, but stands as the unifying beginning. This property of OMA determines the special role of archetypes with an etheric component, treated separately in Chapters 6 and 7.

3.2.2. Correspondence with Known Typologies

The nine fields of the Dar system may be correlated with the categories of known typologies. With the Enneagram [Riso & Hudson, 1999], the nine fields are comparable by the number of basic elements (nine types in the Enneagram). However, the Enneagram organises its nine elements through motivational structures (passions, fixations), whereas the Dars are organised through a functional-elemental principle. The correspondence between concrete elements of the two systems is non-linear and requires its own investigation; some superficial correlations (for instance, between the LOGOS field and Enneagram type 1, the Perfectionist) may prove imprecise or insufficient.

With the Big Five [Costa & McCrae, 1992] the Dar system is correlated through the multi-dimensional articulation of the personality; however, the five-factor Big Five model and the nine-field Dar model employ different principles of identifying their dimensions. The Big Five is grounded in the lexical analysis of linguistic descriptions of personality; the Dars in the authorial ontological intuition.

With MBTI [Briggs Myers et al., 1998] the Dar system is correlated through the combinatorial principle (the triadic Ma–Zhi–Kun code in the Dars, and the four-letter code in MBTI). However, MBTI employs dichotomous axes (E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P), whereas the Dars use nine-valued positions. The difference in combinatorial structure is substantial.

With the Jungian archetypes [Jung, 1959] the fields of the Dars are correlated through the idea of stable psychological patterns possessing a culturally universal grounding. However, the Jungian archetypes (Self, Shadow, Anima, Animus, Wise Old Man, Great Mother, and others) do not form a closed system of a finite number of elements; in Jung, the number and composition of archetypes remain open. In this sense the Dar model is distinguished by a greater formal rigour and completeness.

With Bartle’s typology of players [Bartle, 1996] and its development in Marczewski [Marczewski, 2015], the Dar system is correlated through the function of typological description of user behaviour in the digital environment. Bartle identified four types of players (Achievers, Explorers, Socialisers, Killers); Marczewski, eight. The nine-field Dar model may be regarded as one possible extension of this line, but with a fundamentally different grounding — a deterministic algorithm, rather than self-report or behavioural data.

On the whole, the Dar system is not reducible to any of the typologies enumerated above. It presents an autonomous ontological proposition, drawing upon its own tradition (the investigations of Ya. S. Sibirskiy) and integrable into a wider discussion through the comparisons given.

3.3. The Three Classes of Archetypes: 64 Basic, 16 Integral, 1 Special

3.3.1. The Completeness of the System and Its Internal Articulation

The triadic structure Ma–Zhi–Kun, with each position taking values from 1 to 9, can generate 9 × 9 × 9 = 729 formal combinations. The third position (Kun), however, is computed deterministically from the sum of the first two (see Chapter 4, § 4.1), which reduces the number of distinguishable triplets to 9 × 9 = 81. This number constitutes the complete set of archetypes of the Dar system.

In the authorial system the 81 archetypes do not form a homogeneous list, but fall into three structurally distinct classes:

The basic archetypes (64 in number) — codes Ma–Zhi–Kun in which neither of the first two positions is occupied by the etheric field (value 9).

The integral archetypes (16 in number) — codes of the strict form 9-X-X or X-9-X, in which the etheric field occupies the first or the second position, while one of the basic fields is repeated in the remaining two positions.

The special archetype (1 in number) — the code 9-9-9, in which all three positions are occupied by the etheric field.

Sum: 64 + 16 + 1 = 81. This distribution is mathematically correct (see § 3.3.5) and at the same time substantively meaningful within the authorial system.

Figure 1. The general table of the Dars. [To be inserted at typesetting.]

3.3.2. The Basic Archetypes (64): Structure and Content

The basic class of archetypes is formed by codes Ma–Zhi–Kun in which the first and second positions are occupied by any of the eight basic fields (1–8), while the ninth field (OMA) is absent from these positions. The third position (Kun) is computed deterministically from the first two and may take any value from 1 to 9, including 9.

Substantively, the basic archetypes represent specialised patterns of personality. The word “specialised” here means that within each such archetype a definite combination of concrete functional fields predominates. For example, the bearer of the code 1-6-7 (LOGOS–TUMA–ASTRA) is specialised in the combination structure + movement + word; the bearer of the code 5-3-8 (LUBA–ANDRA–BITRA), in the combination centre + connection + boundaries. In each such archetype, three definite fields operate as the leading fields of the personality, shaping its self-determination and its subsequent life-choices.

Quantitatively, the basic archetypes constitute the majority within the population — approximately 80–85% under a uniform distribution of dates of birth. This is explained by the fact that the probability of the absence of the etheric field (9) in the first two positions is relatively high, and the majority of people prove to be bearers of precisely these basic codes.

It bears specific notice that, within the authorial system, all 64 basic archetypes possess fixed names and symbolic images (visual emblems), elaborated by the principal author of the system (Ya. S. Sibirskiy) over many years of observational and pedagogical work. The name and image of each archetype are not arbitrary; they reflect the essence of the archetype and are fixed within the authorial tradition. The full list of the 64 names is given in Appendix A; the systematic description of each archetype is presented in Chapter 5.

3.3.3. The Integral Archetypes (16): Structure and Content

The integral class of archetypes is formed by codes of the strict form 9-X-X or X-9-X, where X is one of the eight basic fields (1–8), repeated in two contiguous positions. The ninth field (OMA, ether) occupies either the first position (9-X-X) or the second (X-9-X).

Structurally, the integral archetype is characterised by the doubled reinforcement of one basic field in conjunction with the presence of the etheric field. For example:

Code 1-9-1 (LOGOS–OMA–LOGOS): a double presence of the LOGOS field in the Ma and Kun positions, with the etheric OMA in the Zhi position.

Code 9-3-3 (OMA–ANDRA–ANDRA): the etheric field in the Ma position, with a double presence of the ANDRA field in the Zhi and Kun positions.

The complete list of the 16 integral archetypes:

Group 9-X-X (etheric field in the Ma position; basic field repeated in Zhi and Kun): 9-1-1, 9-2-2, 9-3-3, 9-4-4, 9-5-5, 9-6-6, 9-7-7, 9-8-8 — 8 archetypes in total.

Group X-9-X (etheric field in the Zhi position; basic field in Ma and Kun): 1-9-1, 2-9-2, 3-9-3, 4-9-4, 5-9-5, 6-9-6, 7-9-7, 8-9-8 — 8 archetypes in total.

Total: 16 integral archetypes.

Psychologically, the integral archetype of a particular basic field contains within itself all the basic archetypes of that same field. This means that the bearer of an integral archetype — say, of the LOGOS field (1-9-1 or 9-1-1) — potentially conjoins within his or her personality all seven basic archetypes of the LOGOS field, forming an integrative type that exceeds the bounds of the specialised. This property reflects the particular role of the integral archetypes within the Dar system: they represent the type of personality with integrated multiplicity, in contrast to the specialised basic types.

As of the moment of preparation of the present monograph, the 16 integral archetypes have been elaborated and structurally and psychologically described within the authorial tradition of S. N. Nesterova (observational and pedagogical work with their bearers), yet do not possess fixed names and symbolic images, in distinction from the 64 basic archetypes. This is a methodological choice on the part of the authors of the system: the process of symbolic nomination of the integral archetypes requires a longer period of observation, since integrals are encountered more rarely within the population. The corresponding open research task is indicated in the programme of further work.

In Chapter 6 of the present monograph, a systematic description of the 16 integral archetypes is presented in their current state — with their structural code, their psychological content, and their connection with the basic archetypes of the same field.

3.3.4. The Special Archetype (1): Code 9-9-9

The special class is represented by a single archetype, the code 9-9-9 (OMA–OMA–OMA). In this archetype all three positions of the triadic code are occupied by the etheric field; no basic field is present.

Structurally, the archetype 9-9-9 is unique: it is the sole code in which a specialisation in any basic field is absent. Psychologically, it represents a type of pure integrativity without specialisation — not a “structural,” nor a “connecting,” nor a “moving,” nor any other specialised type, but the integral synthesis of all modalities.

Historically and philosophically, the archetype 9-9-9 corresponds most closely to the Jungian conception of the realised Self [Jung, 1959] — the integral centre of the personality that has stepped beyond the bounds of specialised functions. In Jung, the Self is the unattainable ideal of individuation, towards which the development of the personality strives. In the Dar system, 9-9-9 is a real archetype: its bearers are encountered in the population, though rarely.

Quantitatively, the archetype 9-9-9 is encountered in approximately 1% of the population. This is a rare but empirically observable case. According to the observations of the principal author of the system (Ya. S. Sibirskiy), the bearers of the archetype 9-9-9 are distinguished by a particular wholeness without specialisation — which, in the authorial tradition, is designated as the universal integrator of the full type.

In Chapter 7 of the present monograph the archetype 9-9-9 is considered separately, since its status is fundamentally distinct from the status of both the basic and the integral archetypes.

3.3.5. Mathematical Completeness: 81 = 9² as a Closed Set

Mathematically, the distribution 64 + 16 + 1 = 81 is complete: it describes all possible triplets Ma–Zhi–Kun in which the third position is computed as the digital_root of the first two (see Chapter 4).

To verify completeness, the possible configurations may be considered:

If Ma ≠ 9 and Zhi ≠ 9 (8 × 8 = 64 cases), the class of basic archetypes is obtained.

If Ma = 9 and Zhi ≠ 9 (1 × 8 = 8 cases), Kun = digital_root(9 + Zhi) = Zhi. This is the 9-X-X subclass of the integral archetypes.

If Ma ≠ 9 and Zhi = 9 (8 × 1 = 8 cases), Kun = digital_root(Ma + 9) = Ma. This is the X-9-X subclass of the integral archetypes.

If Ma = 9 and Zhi = 9 (1 × 1 = 1 case), Kun = digital_root(18) = 9. This is the archetype 9-9-9.

Sum: 64 + 8 + 8 + 1 = 81.

The completeness of the system means that any possible date of birth yields one of the 81 archetypes; no other possibilities exist within the system. This mathematical property carries an important methodological significance: the model is closed with respect to its input space, which secures its formal correctness, its completeness, and its testability.

3.3.6. Relations between the Classes of Archetypes

Between the three classes of archetypes there exist structural relations, which it is appropriate to describe explicitly.

The basic–integral relation. Each basic field (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) has its own pair of integral archetypes (9-X-X and X-9-X for the corresponding X). Substantively, the integral archetype of the same field figures as the integrated form for all the basic archetypes of that field. This creates a vertical connection: the seven basic archetypes of one field “ascend” into the two integral archetypes of the same field.

The integral–special relation. The 16 integral archetypes represent partial integral forms (with one expressed basic field). The archetype 9-9-9 represents the full integral form (without specialisation). Structurally, 9-9-9 constitutes a kind of “apex” — the sole archetype in which integration is not bound to any specialised basic field.

The basic–special relation. No direct connection exists between the basic archetypes and the archetype 9-9-9: 9-9-9 contains no basic fields within its structure. Substantively, however, the bearer of 9-9-9 potentially includes within his or her integrativity all basic archetypes, since in this code all three positions are occupied by the etheric field, which secures the connection with all basic modalities.

These connections may be presented in the form of a three-level hierarchy, in which each higher level encompasses the lower:

Basic level: 64 specialised archetypes.

Integral level: 16 archetypes, each integrating one of the eight basic fields.

Full integral level: 1 archetype, integrating all fields without specialisation.

This hierarchy reflects the authorial conception that every personality stands in a certain relation to the integral level — as a distant orientation point for some, and as a realised state for others.

3.4. Double Polarity of the Fields: Inner and Outer Elements

3.4.1. The Structural Significance of Double Polarity

The double polarity of the fields, described above in § 3.2.1, requires an additional theoretical unfolding. It constitutes not merely a classificatory device but a structural principle, bearing upon the understanding of the archetypes and upon the mathematics of their comparison.

The principle is formulated as follows:

Each of the four classical elements (earth, air, water, fire) is represented within the Dar system by two fields — one describing its inner aspect, the other its outer. The ninth field (ether) is represented in a single instance and stands outside the paired structure.

This twofoldness reflects an ancient philosophical intuition that any natural or psychological principle possesses an inner (hidden, potential) and an outer (manifest, actual) dimension. This intuition is represented in the tradition of Hesychasm (in the distinction between the “inner man” and the “outer man”), in Hermeticism (in the correspondence between microcosm and macrocosm), in the Indian tradition (in the distinction of the antaryāmin, the inner man, and the subtle body), and in contemporary psychology (in the distinction between internalised and externalised expressions of personality traits).

Within the Dar system the principle of double polarity is employed for:

the organisation of the substantive descriptions of the fields (inner fields are described through introspective phenomenology, outer fields through observable behaviour);

the mathematics of the computation of the opposite archetype (see Chapter 4);

the construction of the empirical control of the Barnum effect (see Chapter 2, § 2.5);

the organisation of relational work with those close to the bearer and the compatibility of archetypes (see Chapter 8).

3.4.2. Mirror Pairs of Fields

The four mirror pairs of fields are as follows:

Pair 1 ↔ 8. LOGOS (inner Earth) and BITRA (outer Earth). Common element: Earth. Distinction: LOGOS is inner structure (rules, foundation); BITRA is outer structure (boundaries, definition).

Pair 2 ↔ 7. NIMA (inner Air) and ASTRA (outer Air). Common element: Air. Distinction: NIMA is inner spaciousness (capacity, multiplicity of variants); ASTRA is outer spaciousness (communication, networks).

Pair 3 ↔ 6. ANDRA (inner Water) and TUMA (outer Water). Common element: Water. Distinction: ANDRA is inner fluidity (empathy, connection); TUMA is outer fluidity (movement, rhythm).

Pair 4 ↔ 5. ZINGRA (inner Fire) and LUBA (outer Fire). Common element: Fire. Distinction: ZINGRA is inner fire (transformation, growth); LUBA is outer fire (centre, will).

The particular field 9. OMA (ether) — without a mirror pair. The principle of integration, represented in a single instance.

3.4.3. The Mirror Operation and Its Mathematics

The principle of double polarity makes it possible to introduce a formal operation of mirror reflection for any field:

mirror(1) = 8, mirror(2) = 7, mirror(3) = 6, mirror(4) = 5, mirror(5) = 4, mirror(6) = 3, mirror(7) = 2, mirror(8) = 1, mirror(9) = 9.

This operation is applied to each position of the triadic code, yielding the opposite archetype. For example:

The archetype 1-6-7 (LOGOS–TUMA–ASTRA), under the mirror operation, yields the archetype 8-3-2 (BITRA–ANDRA–NIMA).

The archetype 5-3-8 (LUBA–ANDRA–BITRA), under the mirror operation, yields 4-6-1 (ZINGRA–TUMA–LOGOS).

The archetype with the wholly etheric code 9-9-9 is its own mirror reflection.

The mirror operation does not preserve the relation Kun = digital_root(Ma + Zhi) in the general case: the opposite archetype is not required to follow the same rule of determination as the original. However, the sum Ma + Zhi in the mirror archetype is equal to (9 − Ma) + (9 − Zhi) = 18 − (Ma + Zhi), and the Kun of the mirror archetype equals the digital_root (the iterative sum of the digits of a number) of this sum. In all cases this yields a correct correspondence among the archetypes existing within the system.

The mirror operation is employed in our empirical work for the construction of the control group of descriptions controlling for the Barnum effect (see Chapter 2, § 2.5, and Chapter 9).

3.5. Comparison of the Dar Model with Known Typologies

For the more precise location of the Dar model within the broader typological landscape, it is appropriate to undertake its comparison with the three largest contemporary typologies (MBTI, the Big Five, the Enneagram) and with one classic of gamification (Bartle’s player types). A summary comparison is presented in Table 3.2.

Brief commentary on the comparison. In comparison with MBTI, the Dars are distinguished by a greater detail of articulation (81 versus 16) and by their principle of determination (a deterministic algorithm versus self-report). MBTI is steadily criticised for its low test-retest reliability (approximately 50% of respondents receive a different type upon repeat administration); within the deterministic Dar model this problem is, in principle, excluded — the code never changes. MBTI, however, possesses a substantially larger base of applied research and an integration into HR practice.

In comparison with the Big Five, the Dars present a categorical typology as against a dimensional one. The Big Five constitutes the mainstream of contemporary academic personality psychology, with high psychometric validity across a wide range of studies [Costa & McCrae, 1992]. The Big Five, however, is poorly adapted to the construction of a digital product: it has no “types” in the ordinary sense. The Dars are oriented towards integration with the digital environment and therefore have a different applied destination.

In comparison with the Enneagram, the Dars are distinguished by a larger number of basic elements (9 fields × 7 basic archetypes in each = 63 basic, plus 16 + 1 = 80; 81 in total). The Enneagram has 9 types plus 27 instinctive subtypes. Structurally, the Enneagram is closer to the Dars than either MBTI or the Big Five: both systems employ 9 basic elements with the possibility of further detailing. The Enneagram, however, is grounded in self-report, whereas the Dars are grounded in a deterministic algorithm.

In comparison with Bartle’s player types, the Dars present a general typology of personality, whereas Bartle’s is a specific typology of gaming behaviour. Yet both systems address the task of the typological description of the user in the digital environment. Bartle has exerted a substantial influence on game design; the Dars, in this part of the task, present a more developed and detailed proposition, oriented not only towards gaming behaviour but towards general self-description.

On the whole, the Dar model occupies a distinct niche within the typological landscape: a deterministic categorical typology of a high degree of detail, oriented towards the digital environment. No direct analogues of this combination of features are known within the contemporary literature.

In the present chapter, the substantive structure of the authorial typological model Dars has been unfolded. The principal positions of the chapter are as follows.

The triadic ontology Ma–Zhi–Kun. The model rests upon the conception of three ontologically distinct levels of the personality: the inner potential (Ma), the outer expression (Zhi), and the point of integration (Kun). This conception inscribes itself within an extensive typological and philosophical tradition of threefold articulation, while preserving the autonomy of its conceptual formulation.

The nine archetypal fields. Each position of the triadic code takes a value from 1 to 9, corresponding to one of the nine fields: LOGOS, NIMA, ANDRA, ZINGRA, LUBA, TUMA, ASTRA, BITRA, OMA. The fields rest upon a double substantive support — functional and elemental; the eight basic fields form four mirror pairs by the principle of inner and outer elements; the ninth field (ether) stands outside the paired structure.

The three classes of archetypes. The complete set of Ma–Zhi–Kun triplets — 81 archetypes — falls into three classes: 64 basic (specialised patterns), 16 integral (doubled reinforcement of one field combined with ether), 1 special (9-9-9, pure integrativity). The sum 64 + 16 + 1 = 81 forms a mathematically closed set describing all possible configurations of the model.

Double polarity. The principle of inner and outer elements establishes the structure of mirror pairs of fields and the formal operation of the opposite archetype, employed in the empirical control of the Barnum effect.

Comparison with known typologies. The Dar model occupies a distinct niche: a deterministic categorical typology of a high degree of detail, oriented towards the digital environment. No direct analogues of this combination of features exist within the contemporary typological literature.

4.1. The Computation of the Triadic Code from the Date of Birth

The algorithm for the generation of an individual profile constitutes a formal procedure by which, from the biographical parameters of the user (in the base case, the date of birth), the personal triadic code in the Dar system is computed. The algorithm is deterministic: identical input parameters always produce an identical output code. This property, discussed in Chapter 3, distinguishes the Dar model from typologies grounded in self-report and secures its formal testability.

This chapter sets out the algorithm formally, examines its properties, and connects it with the model’s multi-level architecture.

The foundation of the algorithm is the classical mathematical operation of the digital root of a natural number. The digital root of a number is defined as the result of the successive summation of its digits until a single-digit result is obtained.

Formally: for a natural number n, its digital root dr(n) is computed as follows:

If n is single-digit (1 ≤ n ≤ 9), then dr(n) = n.

Otherwise, dr(n) = dr(sum of digits of n).

For example:

dr(7) = 7

dr(23) = dr(2 + 3) = dr(5) = 5

dr(999) = dr(9 + 9 + 9) = dr(27) = dr(2 + 7) = dr(9) = 9

dr(1995) = dr(1 + 9 + 9 + 5) = dr(24) = dr(2 + 4) = dr(6) = 6

The digital root possesses a well-known mathematical property: it is equivalent to the remainder of the number’s division by 9, with the exception that, for numbers that are multiples of 9, the digital root equals 9 (not 0). This property is expressed by the formula dr(n) = 1 + ((n − 1) mod 9) for all n ≥ 1.

The digital root is a stable operation known to mathematics since antiquity (the so-called “theosophical reductions” of Pythagorean numerology, analogous operations within Indian mathematics, and the mediaeval “sums of sums” of the Arabic mathematicians). In contemporary mathematics, the digital root is treated within number theory and is employed in algorithms for the verification of divisibility.

Within the Dar system, the digital root is applied as the principal operational instrument, securing the reduction of any biographical numbers (day, month, year) to the standard format of single-digit values 1–9 corresponding to the nine archetypal fields.

4.1.1. The Procedure for Computing an Individual Code

The procedure for the computation of the triadic code Ma–Zhi–Kun from the date of birth consists of three successive steps.

Step 1: computation of the Ma position. The digital roots of the day and month of birth are added, and the digital root of the resulting sum is taken:

Ma = dr(dr(day) + dr(month))

Since for the majority of days and months the digital root coincides with the number itself, in manual computation the simplification

Ma = dr(day + month)

is often admissible. For example, for the date 23 August: Ma = dr(23 + 8) = dr(31) = dr(3 + 1) = dr(4) = 4.

Step 2: computation of the Zhi position. The digital root of the year of birth is taken:

Zhi = dr(year)

For example, for the year 1995: Zhi = dr(1995) = dr(24) = dr(6) = 6.

Step 3: computation of the Kun position. The obtained values of Ma and Zhi are added, and the digital root of the sum is taken:

Kun = dr(Ma + Zhi)

In our example: Kun = dr(4 + 6) = dr(10) = dr(1) = 1.

The resulting code: Ma–Zhi–Kun = 4-6-1.

In the terms of the Dar system, this code corresponds to the archetype ZHAR (4-6-1 — the field ZINGRA in the Ma position, the field TUMA in the Zhi position, the field LOGOS in the Kun position), belonging to the family of basic archetypes of the LOGOS field.

4.1.2. The Formal Notation of the Algorithm

The algorithm may be set out in a formal notation as follows:

Input:  date of birth (D, M, Y), where D ∈ {1..31}, M ∈ {1..12}, Y ∈ {1900..2100}Output: triadic code (Ma, Zhi, Kun), where Ma, Zhi, Kun ∈ {1..9}Step 1: Ma  = dr(dr(D) + dr(M))Step 2: Zhi = dr(Y)Step 3: Kun = dr(Ma + Zhi)where dr(n) = 1 + ((n − 1) mod 9) for n ≥ 1

An alternative functional notation:

(Ma, Zhi, Kun) = (dr(dr(D) + dr(M)), dr(Y), dr(dr(dr(D) + dr(M)) + dr(Y)))

Thus, given a date of birth, the computation of the code reduces to the successive application of the digital-root operation. The procedure is wholly deterministic: no random or subjective factors enter into it.

Let us consider boundary cases and verify the stability of the algorithm.

Minimum date: 1 January 1900. Ma = dr(1 + 1) = 2. Zhi = dr(1900) = dr(10) = 1. Kun = dr(2 + 1) = 3. Code: 2-1-3.

Maximum date (within the typical range): 31 December 2100. Ma = dr(31 + 12) = dr(43) = dr(7) = 7. Zhi = dr(2100) = dr(3) = 3. Kun = dr(7 + 3) = dr(10) = 1. Code: 7-3-1.

A case with multiple reduction: 28 February 1989. Ma = dr(28 + 2) = dr(30) = dr(3) = 3. Zhi = dr(1989) = dr(27) = dr(9) = 9. Kun = dr(3 + 9) = dr(12) = dr(3) = 3. Code: 3-9-3 (an integral archetype of the ANDRA field).

A case yielding the 9-9-9 archetype. To obtain the code 9-9-9, the simultaneous conditions Ma = 9 and Zhi = 9 are required — that is, dr(D + M) = 9 and dr(Y) = 9. For example, 27 December 1989: Ma = dr(27 + 12) = dr(39) = dr(12) = dr(3) — does not qualify. Try 29 April 1989: Ma = dr(29 + 4) = dr(33) = dr(6) — likewise no. A suitable date may be found by requiring D + M divisible by 9: for example, 2 July (D + M = 9), 4 May (9), 11 July (18); whereas 20 October (D + M = 30, dr = 3) does not qualify. Take 2 July 1989: Ma = dr(2 + 7) = 9. Zhi = dr(1989) = 9. Kun = dr(9 + 9) = dr(18) = 9. Code: 9-9-9.

Across all tested cases the algorithm yields a correct result: a triplet whose every position is a single digit from 1 to 9, with the third position computed deterministically from the first two.

4.2. The Multi-level Architecture of the Computation (ODA — TUNA — TRIA — CHIA)

From the base code to the extended profile. The base algorithm described above yields the triadic code Ma–Zhi–Kun — the first level of the user’s profile within the Dar system. The authorial version of the model provides also for an extension of this computation to a four-level architecture, in which to the base triad are added three further strata of the profile. The complete profile of the user within the system is designated by the acronym ODA — TUNA — TRIA — CHIA, after the initial letters of the names of the levels.

In the present monograph we focus principally on the first level (ODA), since it represents the foundation of the model, and its empirical investigation constitutes the principal subject of the work. The further levels are described in an overview form; their detailed theoretical and empirical investigation will constitute the subject of subsequent publications. Within the service application YupDar, however, the algorithm is implemented in its full extent.

ODA — the principal level of the profile. This is the triadic code Ma–Zhi–Kun computed from the date of birth by the procedure described above. ODA determines the user’s belonging to one of the 81 archetypes of the system and constitutes the core of his or her typological profile. In ordinary practice the user of the YupLand ecosystem receives the ODA profile at the very stage of entering the date of birth. The further levels require additional biographical parameters and are activated by the user’s choice.

TUNA — the second level, employing the time of birth (hour and minute). The purpose of this level is to take into account the diurnal context of birth, regarded within the authorial tradition as a parameter additionally characterising the “fine-tuning” of the personality.

The computation of the TUNA level:

Time T = H hours, M minutesTUNA_Ma  = dr(H)TUNA_Zhi = dr(M)TUNA_Kun = dr(TUNA_Ma + TUNA_Zhi)

The full TUNA profile is its own triadic code, analogous in structure to ODA but computed from the time rather than from the date. Substantively, this level is, within the authorial tradition, bound to the temporal aspect of the personality — its relation to rhythms, to the time of day, and to natural cycles.

Since the precise time of birth is not known to all users (especially among generations born prior to the spread of electronic birth records), the TUNA level is optional within our ecosystem. In its absence, the user’s profile is restricted to the principal ODA.

TRIA — the third level, employing the geographical coordinates of the place of birth (latitude and longitude). The purpose is to take into account the spatial context of birth, regarded within the authorial tradition as a parameter reflecting the “geocultural attachment” of the personality.

The computation of the TRIA level is grounded in the digital roots of the values of latitude and longitude (in degrees, to decimal precision, following conversion into standard numerical magnitudes). As in TUNA, the result is its own triadic code. Substantively, this level is bound to the spatial aspect of the personality — its relation to geographical, cultural, and natural contexts.

CHIA — the fourth level, employing the given name and family name of the user. The purpose is to take into account the linguistic and cultural aspect bound to the name as a form of social identification.

The computation of the CHIA level is grounded in a Kabbalistic table of correspondences between the letters of the Cyrillic alphabet and the numbers from 1 to 9. Each letter is assigned a numerical value; the given name and family name are summed letter by letter, and the resulting values are reduced to single-digit values through the digital-root operation. The result is the proper triadic code for the CHIA level.

A particular property of the CHIA level is its variability: the given name and the family name may change in the course of life (upon marriage, change of family name for other reasons, change of given name). This is the sole level among the four that is not strictly determined by the moment of birth.

The full profile of the user within the authorial system is presented as a composition of four triadic codes, one for each level. The authorial tradition also envisages a weighting structure for the interpretation of the profile: the levels differ in their influence upon the current psychological condition of the user.

The basic weighting scheme (as proposed by the author of the system, Ya. S. Sibirskiy):

ODA — 100% (the basic structure of the personality, the foundation of the profile);

TUNA — 70% (a significant additional context);

TRIA — 40% (a spatial context with a lesser direct influence);

CHIA — 20% (the most variable and most peripheral level).

The weights within this scheme do not represent arithmetic multipliers; they are qualitative orientations for interpretation, reflecting the relative stability and basic importance of each level. Their formal grounding and empirical verification constitute the task of future investigations lying beyond the bounds of the present monograph.

The multi-level architecture ODA — TUNA — TRIA — CHIA is a powerful analytical instrument of the authorial system, affording rich possibilities for empirical work. In the present monograph, however, we restrict ourselves to an overview description of this architecture, reserving its detailed elaboration for subsequent works.

The grounds for this decision are the following. The empirical verification of four levels simultaneously requires a substantially more complex research design and a larger sample size than the verification of a single level (ODA). It is appropriate first to fix the results for the base level, and subsequently to extend the analysis. The various levels possess differing data availability: ODA is accessible for any date of birth; TUNA requires the precise time; TRIA, the coordinates of the place of birth; CHIA, the established practice of nomination. The unfolded conceptualisation of the TUNA, TRIA, and CHIA levels requires recourse to themes that exceed the bounds of the present monograph (chronopsychology for TUNA; geographical psychology and cultural anthropology for TRIA; linguistic semantics for CHIA). In the pilot empirical study we obtain stable data only for ODA; data on the other levels are collected optionally and require separate analysis.

4.3. The Properties of the Algorithm: Determinism, Reproducibility, Symmetries

The principal property of the algorithm described is its determinism: given identical input parameters, it always produces an identical output code. This property entails a number of methodological consequences.

Test-retest stability. In typologies grounded in self-report (MBTI, the Enneagram, the Big Five), the typological profile of a person may change upon a repeat administration of the questionnaire. It is known that approximately 50% of those taking MBTI at an interval of several weeks receive a different type [Pittenger, 1993a]. This creates a problem of psychometric reliability for the resolution of which special techniques are required. Within the deterministic Dar model this problem is, in principle, excluded. Since the date of birth does not change, the computed code of the user is stable throughout life. The test-retest reliability of the algorithm equals 1.0 by construction.

Reproducibility. Any researcher possessing access to the user’s date of birth may reproduce the computation independently and obtain the same result. This secures inter-researcher reproducibility, essential for scholarly work.

Transparency. The algorithm is described explicitly and contains no “black boxes,” no machine learning, and no other elements requiring trust in the internal workings of the system. Any person may recompute his or her code manually, on paper, without recourse to software.

An important consequence of the properties of the algorithm is the known theoretical distribution of codes across the population under a uniform distribution of dates of birth. Since the algorithm rests upon the digital root, and the digital root of a number is uniformly distributed within the set {1, 2, …, 9} for random natural numbers across large intervals, the theoretical probability of each of the 81 archetypes may be derived.

The computation of this probability is non-trivial, since dates of birth are not perfectly uniformly distributed (seasonal patterns of birth and demographic effects are well known), and the digital roots of day, month, and year may exhibit correlations. Nevertheless, in a first approximation the following distribution may be expected:

Basic archetypes (64): approximately 79% of the population in aggregate; on average approximately 1.23% per basic archetype.

Integral archetypes (16): approximately 20% of the population in aggregate; on average approximately 1.23% per integral archetype.

Archetype 9-9-9: approximately 1% of the population, since the simultaneous fulfilment of Ma = 9 and Zhi = 9 is required.

The empirical distribution of archetypes within the YupLand sample, given a sufficient volume of data, may be compared with the theoretical. Substantial deviations from the theoretical distribution may indicate selective biases of the sample, substantive particularities of user recruitment, or errors in the algorithm’s implementation. A comparison of the empirical and theoretical distributions will be conducted in Chapter 9.

Within the algorithm, several structural symmetries exist, possessing both a mathematical and a substantive significance.

The Kun symmetry. For two archetypes with the values of Ma and Zhi interchanged, the Kun position coincides. That is, for the code (a, b, c) and the code (b, a, c), the Kun is identical, since dr(a + b) = dr(b + a). This means that any two archetypes with mirror-imaged first two positions belong to a single Kun family (that is, possess one and the same field in the synthesis position). This symmetry lies at the foundation of the organisation of Chapter 5 of the monograph, which describes the basic archetypes by families of fields.

Mirror symmetry. The operation of mirror reflection by polar pairs of fields (1↔8, 2↔7, 3↔6, 4↔5), described in Chapter 3, § 3.4, also possesses a mathematical structure. For an archetype with code (Ma, Zhi, Kun), the mirror archetype has the code (mirror(Ma), mirror(Zhi), mirror(Kun)). This symmetry is employed in the empirical control of the Barnum effect (Chapter 2, § 2.5).

Self-conjugacy of 9-9-9. The archetype 9-9-9 is its own mirror reflection (since mirror(9) = 9). This mathematically distinguishes it as the point of symmetry of the entire system — the sole archetype invariant under the mirror operation.

Symmetries of the integral archetypes. Within the 9-X-X group, each archetype has a “paired” archetype in the X-9-X group with the same basic field X in its doubled occurrence. For example, 9-1-1 and 1-9-1 are the pair of integral archetypes of the LOGOS field, differing only in the position of the etheric component (Ma or Zhi). This symmetry is reflected in the substantive description of the integrals (Chapter 6). The aggregate of these symmetries secures the mathematical beauty of the system.

4.4. The Theoretical Distribution of Archetypes in the Population

The establishment of the theoretical distribution of archetypes across the population is a task of significance both for the assessment of empirical data (through comparison with the expected distribution) and for the understanding of the structure of the model itself.

For the computation we assume a uniform distribution of dates of birth within the population — an approximation reasonable for large samples in the absence of specific demographic effects. The actual distribution of dates of birth in the population exhibits small seasonal fluctuations (it is known that in the Northern Hemisphere a slight peak of births is observed in August–September), but these fluctuations are minor in comparison with the overall volume and produce relatively small distortions of the theoretical probabilities.

The value of Ma is obtained as dr(D + M). For a uniform distribution of dates:

D ∈ {1, 2, …, 31} (adjusted for the length of the month);

M ∈ {1, 2, …, 12}.

The sum D + M ranges over values from 2 (1 January) to 43 (31 December). The distribution of these sums within the population, under uniform dates, is not itself uniform, since differing values of the sum are realised by differing numbers of (D, M) pairs. After the application of the digital root, all values are compressed into the range 1–9. Under a large population volume and uniform dates, the distribution of Ma approaches a uniform distribution within {1, 2, …, 9} — that is, approximately 11.1% per value.

The value of Zhi is obtained as dr(Y), where Y is the year of birth. Since the year is a four-digit number, its digital root is distributed more uniformly than that of one- or two-digit numbers. Under a uniform distribution of years within the sample, Zhi is likewise distributed approximately uniformly within {1, 2, …, 9} — approximately 11.1% per value.

In an actual sample, however, the distribution of years of birth is never uniform: it is shaped by the demographic structure of the population of users. Within the YupLand sample, a predominance of certain age cohorts may be expected (most probably the generations actively using digital services, predominantly 25–55 years of age as of 2026). This may somewhat displace the distribution of Zhi relative to the theoretical.

Kun = dr(Ma + Zhi). If Ma and Zhi are independent and each is uniformly distributed within {1, …, 9}, then the distribution of Kun is likewise uniform. This follows from the properties of modular arithmetic.

Thus, the expected distribution by positions for a sufficiently large sample is as follows:

Ma, uniform: approximately 11.1% per value from 1 to 9.

Zhi, uniform (in the ideal case): approximately 11.1% per value.

Kun, uniform: approximately 11.1% per value.

Under the independence and uniformity of all three positions, the expected probability of each triplet is as follows.

For a basic archetype (Ma ≠ 9, Zhi ≠ 9): P ≈ (1/9) × (1/9) = 1/81 ≈ 1.23%. This is identical for all 64 basic archetypes under the conditions of independence and uniformity.

For an integral archetype of the 9-X-X group (Ma = 9, Zhi = X ≠ 9): P ≈ (1/9) × (1/9) = 1/81 ≈ 1.23% for each of the 8 archetypes of the group. The group in aggregate: 8/81 ≈ 9.88%.

For the X-9-X group: analogously, 8/81 ≈ 9.88%.

For the archetype 9-9-9: P ≈ (1/9) × (1/9) = 1/81 ≈ 1.23%.

In sum: under ideal conditions, each of the 81 archetypes has an expected frequency of approximately 1.23%. The basic archetypes in aggregate yield approximately 64/81 ≈ 79.0%; the integrals, 16/81 ≈ 19.8%; the special archetype, 1/81 ≈ 1.2%.

These theoretical distributions will form the subject of empirical verification in Chapter 9, following the collection of a sufficient sample. The principal testable hypotheses are:

H4.1. The distribution of Ma within the sample is close to uniform (with deviations not exceeding X% per value).

H4.2. The distribution of Zhi within the sample reflects the demographic structure of the sample and may deviate from the uniform.

H4.3. The distribution of Kun, under the uniformity of Ma and Zhi, is uniform.

H4.4. The aggregate distribution across the 81 archetypes corresponds to the expected 1.23% per archetype, with allowance for demographic effects.

Substantial deviations from the theoretical distributions may serve as material for substantive interpretation (for instance, the predominance of certain archetypes among the users of the system as an indicator of which archetypes are more readily inclined to engage with typologies), or may indicate technical problems (errors in the implementation of the algorithm, distortions in the sample).

In the present chapter, the algorithm for the generation of the individual triadic code Ma–Zhi–Kun within the Dar system has been formally described. The principal positions of the chapter are as follows.

The basic operation — the digital root. The algorithm rests upon the classical mathematical operation of the reduction of a multi-digit number to a single digit by the iterative summation of its digits. This operation secures coherence with the system of nine fields and stability for any input data.

The computational procedure. The triadic code is computed in three steps: Ma = dr(day + month), Zhi = dr(year), Kun = dr(Ma + Zhi). The procedure is wholly deterministic, simple for manual computation, and transparent in its structure.

The multi-level architecture. The base code ODA may be extended to a four-level architecture (ODA — TUNA — TRIA — CHIA), including the supplementary strata: the time of birth (TUNA), the geographical coordinates (TRIA), and the given and family names (CHIA). The full architecture constitutes a direction for subsequent research.

The properties of the algorithm. Determinism secures a test-retest stability of 1.0 by construction, together with reproducibility and transparency. Within the algorithm, structural symmetries exist (the Kun symmetry; mirror symmetry by polar pairs of fields; the self-conjugacy of 9-9-9), employed within the empirical design of the investigation.

The theoretical distribution of archetypes. Under uniform input data, each of the 81 archetypes has an expected frequency of approximately 1.23%. The basic archetypes in aggregate constitute approximately 79% of the population; the integrals, approximately 20%; the special archetype, approximately 1%. The empirical distribution within the sample may deviate from the theoretical for demographic reasons; this distribution will be verified in Chapter 9.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The 64 Basic Archetypes: A Systematic Exposition
chapters.html:
The present chapter presents the substantive core of the monograph. Within it, the 64 basic archetypes of the authorial typological model Dars are systematically described. Each archetype receives a compact description according to a unified structure, which secures comparability and ease of comparison.

The descriptions rest upon the primary authorial texts accumulated through the long-standing work of the principal author of the monograph (S. N. Nesterova) with the Dar system. For the purposes of the present work, these texts have been translated from their living artistic register — in which they exist within The Book of DARs and within the YupDar software application — into an academic register. The names of the Dars (LA-DA, ZHAR, ZMAN, and others) are preserved as cultural designations of the authorial tradition; for academic usage each archetype is also given a scientific designation — a neutral functional characterisation of the pattern.

The template of the archetypal description

Each archetype is presented according to a single template:

structural code and name of the Dar (for example, 4-6-1 / ZHAR);

scientific designation of the archetype (for example, “the archetype of the transformer of structures”);

configuration of fields (Ma — Zhi — Kun);

sacred energy — the essence of the archetype in 1–2 sentences;

light side — the optimal expression, in 3–4 sentences;

active shadow — the hypertrophy, with an indication of the deep fear;

passive shadow — the inversion, with an indication of the deep fear;

ecology of realisation — the propitious and the depleting environments;

mission — the teleological summary in a single sentence.

The descriptions are grouped by families of fields. A family is defined by the value of Kun (the third position of the code). Each subsection opens with a general characterisation of the family and a table of the archetypes belonging to it.

The structure of the chapter

5.1. The LOGOS family (Kun = 1) — 7 archetypes

5.2. The NIMA family (Kun = 2) — 7 archetypes

5.9. The OMA family (Kun = 9): the senior archetypes — 8 archetypes

Total: 64 archetypes.

5.1. The LOGOS Family (Kun = 1)

General characterisation of the family. Seven archetypes united by the point of synthesis in the LOGOS field (structure, foundation, cause-and-effect relations). The bearers strive towards the realisation of the structural principle — the construction of support, organisation, form.

LA-DA (2-8-1) — Archetype of the Harmoniser of Boundaries

Configuration: NIMA — BITRA — LOGOS.

Sacred energy. Bringing the inner content of the personality into accord with its outer expression, by working through the boundaries of the psychic and the bodily.

Light side. A steady sense of being at one with oneself. Such a person knows how to bring a situation into harmonious balance and how to work with boundaries without force, yet also without surrender. Others, simply by being near, feel given permission to be themselves.

Active shadow. The pursuit of an ideal balance kills aliveness; the focus on form crowds out the content. Deep fear: losing control over balance.

Passive shadow. A split opens between the inner and the outer, and the bearer can no longer bring them into accord. Deep fear: that the outer can never express the inner.

Ecology. Flourishes in: work with space and design, in the harmonisation of relationships. Wanes in: conflictual environments that allow no fine attunement.

Mission. To coordinate inner content with outer form, securing the wholeness of one’s presence in the world.

I-STOK (3-7-1) — Archetype of the Generator of Flow

Configuration: ANDRA — ASTRA — LOGOS.

Sacred energy. Forming and holding the point from which energy is distributed outwards; the role of the source that fills the field of one’s own presence.

Light side. The bearer feels the inner source as inexhaustible. Generosity comes naturally, and so does the readiness to share. People who spend time with this person come away noticeably revived: in vitality, in motivation, in renewed interest in their work.

Active shadow. The source is drained without replenishment; the bearer feels duty-bound “to feed everyone.” Deep fear: one’s own irreplaceability — that without one, all around will collapse.

Passive shadow. A “drying-out” of the source. Emptiness sets in, and the bearer can fill neither self nor others. Deep fear: that the strength one once felt was only an illusion.

Ecology. Flourishes in: healing practice, mentorship, the founding of organisations. Wanes in: one-sided environments that consume without a return flow.

Mission. To be a conduit of the unbroken flow that fills and renews the vital systems around it.

ZHAR (4-6-1) — Archetype of the Transformer of Structures

Configuration: ZINGRA — TUMA — LOGOS.

Sacred energy. The deep transformation of obsolete structures through the action of intense inner energy: the melting-down of what has frozen, into a new form.

Light side. A stable capacity for radical transformation, a readiness for profound reconsideration. The launching of processes of profound change. Those in contact with the bearer receive access to radical renewal and renounce obsolete patterns.

Active shadow. Heat “without control”: the burning of one’s own and others’ resources; the “spiritual pride of awakening.” Deep fear: of stagnation, of standstill, of petrification.

Passive shadow. A “smouldering”: the heat exists but finds no form; irritability, burnout, sterile rage. Deep fear: that transformation will lead only to destruction.

Ecology. Flourishes in: crisis management, the reform of systems, the psychotherapy of profound transformations. Wanes in: routine without the right to change; within rigid hierarchies.

Mission. To launch processes of profound transformation, by which renewed structures are born from disintegrating forms.

TE-LO (5-5-1) — Archetype of the Integrator of Polarities

Configuration: LUBA — LUBA — LOGOS. A unique archetype within the family, with identical Ma and Zhi.

Sacred energy. The maintenance of a dynamic equilibrium between the two forces of the personality (in the authorial tradition, the “masculine” and the “feminine” principles) and their integration into a third — the creative — principle.

Light side. The harmonious co-existence of the inner polarities; an accord among thoughts, feelings, and actions. The bearer acts as a “single instrument” without inner contradictions. Others perceive him or her as a figure of inner wholeness.

Active shadow. The idealisation of one polarity at the suppression of the other; a narcissistic fixation upon one’s own wholeness. Deep fear: of the disturbance of the inner balance as a threat to the foundation of the personality.

Passive shadow. The disintegration of the polarities: a rupture between the “masculine” and the “feminine”; an estrangement from the body or from the “spiritual” side. Deep fear: that inner wholeness is in principle unattainable.

Ecology. Flourishes in: bodily practices, craft, art; in work with the wholeness of clients. Wanes in: professions requiring the renunciation of one side of the personality.

Mission. To embody the inner harmony of the polarities within outer action.

SVE-TO (6-4-1) — Archetype of the Vital Impulse

Configuration: TUMA — ZINGRA — LOGOS.

Sacred energy. The production of a substantial quantity of vital energy radiated into the outer world; the filling of space with a vitalising force.

Light side. A stably high level of vital tone; swift restoration; resistance to apathy. The bearer enlivens the environment — accelerating processes, charging others. Those around experience an inflow of forces, a desire to act.

Active shadow. A “shining for others” with the neglect of oneself; the sense of messianism; “toxic positivity.” Deep fear: of dimming, of invisibility.

Passive shadow. A “fading”: chronic fatigue and apathy alien to one’s own nature. Deep fear: that the radiance has been a temporary gift.

Ecology. Flourishes in: education, leadership, motivational practice, the psychotherapy of depressive disorders. Wanes in: isolated work without feedback; within environments of chronic negativism.

Mission. To radiate vital force, awakening it in others, and to sustain within the surrounding space the level of energy necessary for productive processes.

PRI-TOK (7-3-1) — Archetype of the Accumulator of Resource

Configuration: ASTRA — ANDRA — LOGOS.

Sacred energy. The gathering of energy from the outer space and the formation of the point of its concentration; the role of the accumulator in which scattered flows fold into a concentrated resource.

Light side. The capacity for deep replenishment through contact with outer sources; stability through accumulation rather than through direct production. The creation of places and contexts in which energy is concentrated. Those around obtain access to the concentrated resource through contact with the bearer.

Active shadow. A one-sided accumulation without return; in extreme forms, an “energetic vampirism” in relation to people in place of reliance upon impersonal sources. Deep fear: of depletion, of the loss of what has been accumulated.

Passive shadow. A paralysed capacity for gathering; a chronic emptiness in the formal presence of sources. Deep fear: of the impossibility of self-sufficiency.

Ecology. Flourishes in: the creation of “places of power,” cultural centres, ecological practice. Wanes in: purely productive work without accumulation.

Mission. To gather scattered flows into concentrated points, rendering the accumulated resource accessible to others.

LE-LI (8-2-1) — Archetype of the Connection with Nature

Configuration: BITRA — NIMA — LOGOS.

Sacred energy. The deep connection with the fundamental natural rhythms and structures — bodily, ancestral, biological; the restoration of natural rightness.

Light side. A stable sense of connection with one’s own body and with the general biological order; the capacity to attune to natural rhythms. Work with fundamental structures — bodily, ancestral, environmental. Those in contact with the bearer restore the connection with their roots, with their nature.

Active shadow. The idealisation of the natural and the archaic at the rejection of the contemporary; an excessive density, inertia, the idealisation of the past. Deep fear: of the loss of connection with the fundamental ground.

Passive shadow. The interrupted connection with the natural ground; the feeling of superficiality, of being torn from the body. Deep fear: that one’s own ground has been illusory.

Ecology. Flourishes in: bodily practices, ecologically oriented activity, ancestral therapy. Wanes in: purely abstract contexts; under the violation of biological rhythms.

Mission. To restore the personality’s connection with its natural and ancestral ground.

5.2. The NIMA Family (Kun = 2)

General characterisation of the family. Seven archetypes with the point of synthesis in the NIMA field (spaciousness, the holding of contradictions, the potential of multiplicity). The bearers strive towards the realisation of spaciousness — both inner and outer — and of the capacity to hold multidimensionality without reducing it to one.

BRA-MA (1-1-2) — Archetype of the Holding of the Primordial Principle

Configuration: LOGOS — LOGOS — NIMA. A unique archetype within the family, with identical Ma and Zhi.

Sacred energy. Holding fundamental principles and primordial origins within a field of multidimensionality; sustaining the foundation upon which any potential may unfold.

Light side. The bearer can hold fundamental principles without collapsing them into the particular. He or she creates a stable ground within which a multiplicity of expressions becomes possible. Those nearby gain a support from which their own processes may unfold.

Active shadow. Principles harden into dogma. The foundation becomes a wall that admits no development. Deep fear: that without rigid holding, everything will fall apart.

Passive shadow. The support is lost; principles can no longer be held; the bearer dissolves into multiplicity without ground. Deep fear: that one’s own holding has only ever been illusory.

Ecology. Flourishes in: the fundamental disciplines, in work with primordial principles (mathematics, philosophy, the basic sciences). Wanes in: a constant superficial churn of paradigms.

Mission. To hold the primordial principles, so that multiple development becomes possible upon them.

GO-RA (3-8-2) — Archetype of the Ascending Potential

Configuration: ANDRA — BITRA — NIMA.

Sacred energy. The accumulation of potential through emotional connection and its ascent in the form of a stable, protected structure; an inner growth akin to the growth of a mountain.

Light side. The capacity for gradual, many-yeared accumulation of inner potential; stability, monumentality. The creation of protected spaces for one’s own and others’ growth. Those around perceive the bearer as a “mountain” — steady, unaffected by passing influences.

Active shadow. A heaviness, an immobility; a protection so firm that it blocks contact. Deep fear: of the destruction of the accumulated form.

Passive shadow. The erosion of what has been accumulated, the inability to protect what has been achieved; the “destruction of the mountain from within.” Deep fear: that the accumulation has been in vain.

Ecology. Flourishes in: long-term projects requiring endurance (the sciences, the arts of culture, ancestral inheritance). Wanes in: rapid changes without the possibility of accumulation.

Mission. To create ascending structures of stable potential, upon which others may lean.

GU-NA (4-7-2) — Archetype of the Balancing of Qualities

Configuration: ZINGRA — ASTRA — NIMA.

Sacred energy. The fine attunement of the qualitative characteristics of a situation, of relationships, of an environment; work with the guṇas — the subtle modes of manifestation — through speech and through transformation.

Light side. Sensitivity to qualitative shadings; the capacity for fine attunement through speech and through small transforming actions. The bearer works as a “tuner” — bringing situations into their optimal tonality. Those around feel that “all has fallen into place.”

Active shadow. An excessive fine attunement turning into manipulation; an artificial harmonisation at the expense of authentic needs. Deep fear: of crude, unrefined reality.

Passive shadow. The inability of attunement; an immersion in the chaos of qualitative shadings without the possibility of ordering them. Deep fear: of one’s own incompetence in the sphere of subtlety.

Ecology. Flourishes in: work with sound, voice, fine communication; in the arts and in diplomacy. Wanes in: coarse environments demanding not attunement but forceful action.

Mission. To tune the qualitative tonalities of the environment, rendering it suitable for subtle processes.

SO-NA (5-6-2) — Archetype of Inner Sounding

Configuration: LUBA — TUMA — NIMA.

Sacred energy. The sounding of the inner centre in the rhythm of outer movement; the transformation of the volitional impulse into a harmonic oscillation filling the space.

Light side. An inner centre that “sounds”: the bearer’s presence resonates with the surrounding environment without dominating it. The capacity to lead through sounding rather than through pressure. Those around feel “an attunement to a single wavelength” in the bearer’s presence.

Active shadow. A resonant intrusiveness; the “tuning” of the surroundings to one’s own tonality without regard for their needs. Deep fear: of one’s own “soundlessness,” of going unnoticed.

Passive shadow. An inner “soundlessness”: the inability to express oneself in harmonic resonance; deafness to one’s own centre. Deep fear: of the absence of response.

Ecology. Flourishes in: music, vocal practice, team work grounded in attunement. Wanes in: noisy competitive environments that drown out subtle sounding.

Mission. To sound from one’s own centre in resonance with the world, rendering the space suitable for harmonic interaction.

U-MA (6-5-2) — Archetype of the Receptacle of Meaning

Configuration: TUMA — LUBA — NIMA.

Sacred energy. The holding of a broad semantic field in the presence of a stable centre; the work of the mind as a space within which meanings have place without competition.

Light side. A volumetric thinking in which various meanings co-exist; a centred attention that does not reduce multiplicity. The capacity to lead intellectual processes without losing breadth of scope. Those in contact obtain access to a more capacious picture.

Active shadow. Intellectual expansion: the attempt to draw all meanings into one’s own system. Deep fear: of intellectual incompetence.

Ecology. Flourishes in: individual creative work, authorial projects. Wanes in: excessively structured environments with imposed rhythm.

Mission. To hold one’s own rhythm of self-awareness as the foundation of authentic development.

TA-RA (7-8-6) — Archetype of the Master of Transformations

Configuration: ASTRA — BITRA — TUMA.

Sacred energy. The art of being the connecting link — consciously assuming and setting aside roles and forms in order to put into motion the exchange of energy, information, and connection between people and worlds.

Light side. A master of bridges and exchange: the bearer senses which form must be assumed here and now to set resources in motion, adapting fluidly to context — as merchant, diplomat, actor, communicator. The strength lies in conscious flexibility: knowing when to be businesslike and when soft, and when to set aside one role’s costume in time to put on another.

Active shadow. “Social restlessness”: the conscious changing of roles passes into chaotic play; masks change so swiftly that contact with one’s own essence is lost. Deep fear: that one’s real face will be rejected — the endless changing creates the illusion of safety yet renders the bearer ungraspable even to himself or herself.

Passive shadow. “Prisoner of a role”: the bearer becomes stuck in a single social or professional role and cannot set it aside even when it has grown foreign — the strict manager at home as at work, the one frozen in the role of “victim.” Deep fear: of losing one’s footing without the familiar mask; the role displaces life.

Ecology. Flourishes in: sales, negotiation, diplomacy; acting, public speaking, media; coaching and role-based psychology; event management and the building of network interactions; trade and brokering. Wanes in: rigidly regulated environments demanding the same person in every situation; total isolation; contexts of double standards; severe stress that leaves no energy for conscious adaptation.

Mission. To be a living channel of exchange — wearing the roles with mastery while preserving the inner core and the clear knowledge of who one is when all the costumes are set aside.

SO-KHA (8-7-6) — Archetype of the Forming Word

Configuration: BITRA — ASTRA — TUMA.

Sacred energy. A protected form unfolded through the word and moving in the flow; speech that forms structures through time.

Light side. The capacity, through the word, to create stable forms in time; the “word made reality.” Those in contact perceive: “these words form the future.”

Active shadow. A compulsory formation through speech; rigid speech-constructions. Deep fear: that without speech the form will not arise.

Passive shadow. The loss of the forming force of the word; a speech leaving no trace. Deep fear: of one’s own speech-helplessness.

Ecology. Flourishes in: legislation, strategic declarations, literary art. Wanes in: environments that devalue the word.

Mission. To form stable structures through the word, passing through time.

The bearers strive towards the realisation of the connective principle through communication — the building of paths of meaning-transmission among heterogeneous systems.

Z-MAN (1-6-7) — Archetype of the Keeper of Time

Configuration: LOGOS — TUMA — ASTRA.

Sacred energy. A structure unfolded in the flow of time and gathered into the form of speech; the “serpent of time” binding moments into a meaningful sequence.

Light side. The capacity to perceive the structural succession of events within the flow of time; speech that renders the temporal connections visible. Those in contact gain the sense of the “historical dimension” of what is happening.

Active shadow. A hypertrophy of temporal vision; an “everything has been before, nothing is new.” Deep fear: of the loss of historical connectedness.

Passive shadow. The loss of sensitivity to temporal connections; life lived “outside history.” Deep fear: that time is meaningless.

Ecology. Flourishes in: historical, analytical, and strategic disciplines. Wanes in: environments of exclusive focus upon the “here and now.”

Mission. To hold the structural connectedness of time, rendering it visible through speech.

BRA-KH-MA (2-5-7) — Archetype of the Universal Mind

Configuration: NIMA — LUBA — ASTRA.

Sacred energy. A spaciousness of consciousness, centred at the volitional point and expressed through the word; the “universal mind,” accessible for one’s own use and for that of others.

Light side. Volumetric thinking with centred will; the capacity, through the word, to disclose the “universal dimension” of questions. Those in contact gain access to a more capacious picture.

Active shadow. Intellectual expansion; a “universality” that leaves no place for the particular. Deep fear: of intellectual limitation.

Passive shadow. The loss of the capacity for universal thinking; narrowness. Deep fear: that the universal is unattainable.

Ecology. Flourishes in: philosophical, theoretical, educational activity. Wanes in: purely applied, narrow tasks.

Mission. To realise the universal mind as the side of thought made accessible through speech.

GRAD (3-4-7) — Archetype of the Builder of Communities

Configuration: ANDRA — ZINGRA — ASTRA.

Sacred energy. A warm connection transformed into action and given form through speech; the “city” as the structure within which a community lives.

Light side. The capacity to create communities — through warm connection, transformation, precise speech. Those in contact receive an invitation “into the city” — into a common space.

Active shadow. A hyper-building; the transformation of a community into an institution. Deep fear: of the disintegration of the community.

Passive shadow. The impossibility of building a community; solitude. Deep fear: that community is, in principle, impossible.

Ecology. Flourishes in: the founding of organisations, movements, cultural centres. Wanes in: individualistic contexts.

Mission. To build living communities through connection, transformation, and precise speech.

AR-KHEY (4-3-7) — Archetype of the Primordial Principle of Speech

Configuration: ZINGRA — ANDRA — ASTRA.

Sacred energy. A transformative force, warmth, and the word, gathered into the first principle — the point from which meaningful speech arises.

Light side. The capacity to find the “first word” — the formulation that opens a new understanding. A creative interaction with the word. Those in contact gain access to “primordial” formulations.

Active shadow. A hypertrophy of creativity; a constant reformulation without stable support. Deep fear: of the “wearing-out” of words.

Passive shadow. The loss of the capacity for the primordial; speech that is borrowed and not one’s own. Deep fear: of one’s own speech-secondariness.

Ecology. Flourishes in: literature, philosophy, poetic work. Wanes in: formalised, repetitive speech environments.

Mission. To return speech to its primordial origin, opening new possibilities of understanding.

NI-RA (5-2-7) — Archetype of High Simplicity

Configuration: LUBA — NIMA — ASTRA.

Sacred energy. A centre unfolded within spaciousness and expressed through simple speech; “high simplicity” as a matured attainment.

Light side. The capacity for simple, clear, non-reductive speech; high simplicity as a quality. Those in contact feel: “all has become understandable without loss of depth.”

Active shadow. An excessive simplification; high simplicity passing into flatness. Deep fear: of being misunderstood.

Passive shadow. The impossibility of attaining simplicity; speech remains entangled. Deep fear: that simplicity is unattainable.

Ecology. Flourishes in: didactic, philosophical, journalistic activity. Wanes in: complexifying, academically closed environments.

Mission. To realise high simplicity as the mature quality of speech.

MA-NA (6-1-7) — Archetype of Spiritual Nourishment

Configuration: TUMA — LOGOS — ASTRA.

Sacred energy. A flow set within a structure and transmitted through speech; “manna” as the food that falls at the needed moment.

Light side. The capacity to give through speech “what is needed now” — the right word at the right moment. Those in contact receive “nourishment” in difficult periods.

Active shadow. A hypertrophy of the “nourishing” function; an obsessive speaking “for others.” Deep fear: of one’s own uselessness.

Passive shadow. The loss of the capacity to “nourish” through the word; speech does not nourish. Deep fear: that words have never been food.

Ecology. Flourishes in: spiritual, psychotherapeutic, mentoring practice. Wanes in: environments that do not envisage “nourishment” through speech.

Mission. To be spiritual nourishment through the word that falls at the needed moment.

PRA-NA (8-8-7) — Archetype of Vital Breath

Configuration: BITRA — BITRA — ASTRA. A unique archetype within the family, with identical Ma and Zhi.

Sacred energy. A doubled protected form expressed through the word; prāṇa as the vital breath given form in speech.

Light side. The capacity, through the word, to “breathe life” into forms; speech that vivifies structures. Those in contact feel that “all has come alive.”

Active shadow. A hypertrophy of “breathing-in”; an obsessive enlivening. Deep fear: of the lifelessness of forms.

Passive shadow. The loss of the capacity to “breathe life”; forms remain dead. Deep fear: of one’s own speech-helplessness.

Ecology. Flourishes in: creative, pedagogical, spiritual activity. Wanes in: lifelessly formal environments.

Mission. To breathe life into forms through the word, rendering them living.

5.8. The BITRA Family (Kun = 8)

The bearers strive towards the realisation of the form-giving principle — the establishment of contours, the protection of what is held within them, and the giving of form to potential.
