BI-RA (1-7-8) — Archetype of the Lawgiver of Reality

Configuration: LOGOS — ASTRA — BITRA.

Sacred energy. The architecture of meaning: the capacity to crystallise rules out of the chaos of ideas, to give them life through the spoken word, and to safeguard them within clear, reliable boundaries.

Light side. The architect of agreements: the bearer turns abstract justice into living law, building unshakeable structures out of the chaos of opinions. He or she finds the precise words by which rules are heard by the heart, and creates the space within which they gain force. Where others see only the quarrel about “how things ought to be,” the bearer builds a working mechanism of reality — transparent, protected, intelligible to all.

Active shadow. “The manipulator of laws”: the bearer weaves tangled rules to control others, finding loopholes within his or her own agreements; words confuse rather than clarify; boundaries are set for everyone but the bearer. Deep fear: that honest rules will strip away one’s edge and leave one exposed.

Passive shadow. “The dreamer-theorist”: a perfect system lives in the bearer’s head, yet cannot be given outer structure; he or she dares not speak it aloud for fear of criticism, and brilliant designs remain useless thoughts. Deep fear: that the rules will shatter against reality or under critique.

Ecology. Flourishes in: the drafting of clear contracts and statutes; the installation of simple, fair rules within teams; the work of the methodologist mapping and documenting processes; the role of the arbitrator or mediator; the parental establishment of healthy, clearly drawn boundaries. Wanes in: full anarchy where any rule is rejected in principle; rigid totalitarian systems in which all has been decided; situations demanding instantaneous reaction without space for the agreement of rules; the company of those who on principle do not honour agreements.

Mission. To set the rules of a game in which all are willing to play — to act as the fair judge and the architect, raising clear and dependable rules of the road by which the common life may move forward in safety.

SO-LAR (2-6-8) — Archetype of the Solar Contour

Configuration: NIMA — TUMA — BITRA.

Sacred energy. A spaciousness moving in the flow of time and gathered into a radiating contour; the sun possessed of boundaries.

Light side. The capacity to radiate within clearly drawn boundaries; “solar” energy with protection. Those in contact receive a warm radiance that does not scorch.

Active shadow. An excessive protection of the radiance; the sun hidden behind a wall. Deep fear: of dimming.

Passive shadow. The loss of the contour; a radiance scattering without control. Deep fear: of one’s own inadequacy as a “sun.”

Ecology. Flourishes in: public activity, the role of the public face of an organisation. Wanes in: environments demanding either concealment or full disclosure.

Mission. To radiate within a clear contour, rendering one’s own presence at once visible and protected.

KO-DA (3-5-8) — Archetype of the Coding Form

Configuration: ANDRA — LUBA — BITRA.

Sacred energy. A warm connection centred at the volitional point and given form as a structural code; the form coding what is of value.

Light side. The capacity to create “codes” — formed structures that transmit living content. The creation of systems in which meaning is preserved through form. Those in contact receive the “keys” to what is of value.

Active shadow. A hypertrophy of coding; the transformation of the living into a cipher. Deep fear: of the loss of content.

Passive shadow. The inability to code; meaning disperses without form. Deep fear: that the code has been an illusion.

Ecology. Flourishes in: systems development, the architecture of knowledge, the encoding of meanings of value. Wanes in: environments of direct, unstructured communication.

Mission. To encode living content into a form that secures its preservation and transmission.

LI-KO (4-4-8) — Archetype of the Manifested Visage

Configuration: ZINGRA — ZINGRA — BITRA. A unique archetype within the family, with identical Ma and Zhi.

Sacred energy. A doubled transformative force given form as a protected visage; the “visage” as the manifested expression of the inner fire.

Light side. The capacity to manifest one’s own transformed inner visage in a clear, protected form. Those in contact see the “true face” of the bearer.

Active shadow. An excessive manifestation; a hypertrophy of the visage without inner support. Deep fear: of the loss of face.

Passive shadow. The loss of the capacity to manifest; the visage is effaced. Deep fear: of one’s own facelessness.

Ecology. Flourishes in: public, artistic, and spiritual activity. Wanes in: environments requiring anonymity.

Mission. To manifest one’s own transformed visage in a clear and protected form.

ZLA-TO (5-3-8) — Archetype of Value in Protection

Configuration: LUBA — ANDRA — BITRA.

Sacred energy. A centre warmed by connection and set within a protected, precious form; “gold” as the value requiring protection.

Light side. The capacity to recognise and to protect what is of value; an inner value of one’s own, set within a stable contour. Those around perceive the bearer as a “person of value.”

Active shadow. A hypertrophy of the protection of what is precious; an avarice that turns protection into miserliness. Deep fear: of the loss of what is precious.

Passive shadow. The inability to protect what is of value; devaluation. Deep fear: that the value has been illusory.

Ecology. Flourishes in: work with cultural heritage, the management of resources, expertise concerning what is of value. Wanes in: environments that devalue the particular.

Mission. To recognise and to protect what is of value within a stable form.

BI-MA (6-2-8) — Archetype of Rhythmic Protection

Configuration: TUMA — NIMA — BITRA.

Sacred energy. A flow unfolded in spaciousness and given form as a protective shape; protection possessed of its own rhythm.

Light side. The capacity to protect rhythmically — cyclically, at the needed moments, with a sense of time. Those around receive “a protection that knows when it is needed.”

Active shadow. An excessive rhythmic protection; a permanent defensive posture. Deep fear: of missing the moment of attack.

Passive shadow. The loss of the rhythm of protection; the defence arrives “not at the right time.” Deep fear: of one’s own imprecision in defence.

Ecology. Flourishes in: long-term guarding and protective activity with a cyclical sense. Wanes in: environments demanding constant mobilisation.

Mission. To realise rhythmic protection synchronised with the flow of time.

MI-DA (7-1-8) — Archetype of Meaningful Measure

Configuration: ASTRA — LOGOS — BITRA.

Sacred energy. A word organised within structure and set within a protected measure; the “word of measure” as the boundary of meaning.

Light side. The capacity, through the word, to establish meaningful limits; clarity in determining “what this is.” Those in contact receive a clear definition.

Active shadow. A rigid determination; a word that admits no expansion of meaning. Deep fear: of blurring.

Passive shadow. The loss of the capacity for measure; words lose precision. Deep fear: that measure is in principle impossible.

Ecology. Flourishes in: legislation, academic work, expertise. Wanes in: environments that deny clear definitions.

Mission. To establish meaningful measure through the word set within a protected structure.

5.9. The OMA Family (Kun = 9): The Senior Archetypes

General characterisation of the family. Eight archetypes that differ from the rest of the families: their Ma and Zhi occupy basic fields (1–8), yet the point of synthesis is found within the etheric field OMA (9). The authorial tradition names these archetypes the senior archetypes: their specialised pattern (determined by Ma and Zhi) develops in the direction of integral wholeness (determined by Kun = 9). This does not make them integral in the strict sense (see Chapter 6), but places them in a particular relation to the other families. Numerically the family contains 8 archetypes rather than 7 — a mathematical consequence of the algorithm (see Chapter 4, § 4.4).

RAY (1-8-9) — Archetype of the Protected Whole

Configuration: LOGOS — BITRA — OMA.

Sacred energy. Structure given form within a protected boundary, then integrated into the whole; “paradise” as an ordered, protected space that bears a common meaning.

Light side. The bearer can create protected wholistic spaces — structures in which nothing disturbs the common wholeness. Those who enter such a space find what feels like an “island of order.”

Active shadow. Wholeness becomes hyper-guarded. The “paradise” turns into a place where outer influences are forbidden. Deep fear: of any violation of the whole.

Passive shadow. The protected whole cannot be built; what remains is a “lost paradise.” Deep fear: that wholeness itself is impossible.

Ecology. Flourishes in: the creation of communities, gardens, cultural spaces. Wanes in: open competitive environments.

Mission. To create a protected whole in which everything is in its place.

FA-NA (2-7-9) — Archetype of Dissolution in the Whole

Configuration: NIMA — ASTRA — OMA.

Sacred energy. A spaciousness unfolded through the word and integrated into etheric unity; fanā as the dissolution of the individual within the common.

Light side. The capacity for the dissolution of the individual position within the common field without the loss of self; speech as a bridge between the “I” and the “All.” Those in contact receive the experience of unity.

Active shadow. Excessive dissolution; the loss of self within the “common.” Deep fear: of being “separate.”

Passive shadow. The impossibility of dissolution; a rigid separateness. Deep fear: that unity is impossible.

Ecology. Flourishes in: spiritual practices, meditative groups, philosophical work with consciousness. Wanes in: environments demanding a rigid individual position.

Mission. To realise dissolution in the common as a form of deep integration.

IRIY (3-6-9) — Archetype of the Flowing Unity

Configuration: ANDRA — TUMA — OMA.

Sacred energy. A warm connection unfolded in the flow of time and integrated into etheric wholeness; Iriy as the paradisal space in which all flows within a common current.

Light side. The capacity to hold connection within the flow of time and to raise it to the level of the common; “all is connected within all time.” Those in contact receive the experience of the long connection.

Active shadow. The idealisation of the past as a “lost Iriy.” Deep fear: of the rupture of the flow.

Passive shadow. The loss of sensitivity to flowing unity. Deep fear: that connection does not exist in time.

Ecology. Flourishes in: work with memory, tradition, lineage, historical depth. Wanes in: wholly present-oriented environments.

Mission. To hold connection across the entire flow of time, raising it to the common level.

SHI-VA (4-5-9) — Archetype of the Transforming Centre

Configuration: ZINGRA — LUBA — OMA.

Sacred energy. A transformation centred at the volitional point and integrated into the common whole; the centre through which universal transformation occurs.

Light side. The capacity to lead through great transformations with centred will and a common perspective. Those in contact gain access to “universal” transformation.

Active shadow. Hyper-transformation; destruction in the name of renewal. Deep fear: of the cessation of transformation.

Passive shadow. The loss of transforming force; the centre without transformation. Deep fear: that transformation has been an illusion.

Ecology. Flourishes in: radical leadership, work with great transitions, spiritual transformation. Wanes in: stable, non-transforming environments.

Mission. To lead universal transformation through centred will.

MI-RA (5-4-9) — Archetype of the Peacemaking Will

Configuration: LUBA — ZINGRA — OMA.

Sacred energy. A centre transforming through volitional action and integrated into the common whole; mir as a state held through will.

Light side. The capacity to hold peace through volitional action; a centred will directed at the common good. Those in contact receive the experience of “peace as an attainment.”

Active shadow. A compulsory peace; a will imposing the common. Deep fear: of the disintegration of peace.

Passive shadow. The loss of the peacemaking will; “peace” slips away. Deep fear: that peace is, in principle, unattainable.

Ecology. Flourishes in: diplomacy, high politics, the facilitation of complex conflicts. Wanes in: environments that do not envisage peacemaking action.

Mission. To realise the will that holds the common peace.

TOT (6-3-9) — Archetype of Knowledge in the Flow

Configuration: TUMA — ANDRA — OMA.

Sacred energy. A flow warmed by connection and integrated into etheric wholeness; Thoth as the figure of the sage holding knowledge across time.

Light side. The capacity to accumulate and to transmit knowledge through the long flow of time; the connection of generations through knowledge. Those in contact receive a “hologram of knowledge.”

Active shadow. Self-positioning as “the sole bearer of knowledge.” Deep fear: of the loss of knowledge with death.

Passive shadow. The loss of sensitivity to knowledge; dispersal. Deep fear: that knowledge has been an illusion.

Ecology. Flourishes in: academic, museum, library activity; in the role of the “keeper” of knowledge. Wanes in: environments that devalue historical knowledge.

Mission. To hold knowledge through the long flow of time, securing its transmission.

TO-RA (7-2-9) — Archetype of the Teaching Word

Configuration: ASTRA — NIMA — OMA.

Sacred energy. A word unfolded within spaciousness and integrated into the common whole; the Torah as the teaching text bearing universal significance.

Light side. The capacity to give a teaching word possessing force for a wide field; speech addressed to all. Those in contact receive a “teaching text.”

Active shadow. A hypertrophy of the teaching function; “preaching.” Deep fear: of being unheard.

Passive shadow. The loss of the teaching function; speech without address. Deep fear: that the teaching has been out of place.

Ecology. Flourishes in: pedagogical, spiritual-teaching activity. Wanes in: environments that deny the teaching function.

Mission. To give the teaching word possessing significance for a wide field.

ROY (8-1-9) — Archetype of the Structural Multitude

Configuration: BITRA — LOGOS — OMA.

Sacred energy. A protected form organised within a structure and integrated into etheric wholeness; the swarm as a multitude acting as one.

Light side. The capacity to see the multitude as an organised whole; work with great systems as with a single being. Those in contact receive a “systemic vision.”

Active shadow. A dissolution within the collective; a “swarm consciousness” without individual voice. Deep fear: of the loss of the collective structure.

Passive shadow. The inability to see the multitude as a whole; fragmentariness. Deep fear: that the collective has been an illusion.

Ecology. Flourishes in: systems analysis, the management of great systems, collective projects. Wanes in: strictly individualistic environments.

Mission. To see and to hold the multitude as a structural whole.

Chapter Summary

In the present chapter, the 64 basic archetypes of the Dar model have been systematically described, grouped into nine families by the Kun position. Each archetype has received a unified description according to the eight-position template: structural code, name of the Dar, scientific designation of the archetype, configuration of fields, sacred energy, light side, active and passive shadows with their deep fears, ecology of realisation, mission.

The names of the Dars have been preserved as cultural designations of the authorial tradition (LA-DA, I-STOK, ZHAR, TE-LO, SVE-TO, PRI-TOK, LE-LI for the LOGOS family, and analogously for the others). For academic usage each archetype has additionally been assigned a scientific designation — a neutral functional characterisation of the pattern.

The descriptions rest upon primary authorial texts systematised in The Book of DARs and within the YupLand digital ecosystem, and have been translated into the academic register with preservation of their semantic content.

The following chapter examines the 16 integral archetypes — a separate class distinguished from the basic by the doubled reinforcement of a single basic field and the presence of an etheric component.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The 16 Integral Archetypes
chapters.html:
The present chapter is devoted to the second class of archetypes within the Dar system — the integral archetypes. Integrals differ from the basic archetypes (Chapter 5) both structurally and psychologically. The structural difference consists in a particular configuration of the triadic code: integral archetypes possess codes of the strict form 9-X-X or X-9-X, where X is one of the eight basic fields (1–8), while the Ma or Zhi position is occupied by the etheric field OMA (value 9). The psychological difference consists in the particular functional nature of such archetypes: the integral archetype of a definite basic field contains within itself all the basic archetypes of the same field, combining their specialised patterns into a wider, integrated type.

The present chapter sets out the 16 integral archetypes in detail, treats their structural definition, psychological function, and relation to the basic archetypes of the corresponding fields, and indicates the open research task — the symbolic nomination of the integrals — which, at the time of writing, remains unresolved.

Structure of the chapter:

6.1. The structural definition of the integral archetype

6.2. The psychological function of the integral

6.3. The relation of the integral archetype to the basic archetypes of the same field

6.4. A systematic exposition of the 16 integral archetypes

6.5. The open task of symbolic nomination

6.1. The Structural Definition of the Integral Archetype

The integral archetype within the Dar system is defined by a formal condition upon the triadic code Ma–Zhi–Kun. The condition is the following: one of the two “biographically computed” positions (Ma or Zhi) is occupied by the etheric field (value 9), while the remaining “computed” position is occupied by a basic field X (a value from 1 to 8). Under this distribution, the third position (Kun) is determined deterministically and proves equal to X (by the properties of the digital root; see Chapter 4).

From this follow two structural groups of integral archetypes:

Group 9-X-X (etheric field in the Ma position; basic field X in the Zhi and Kun positions): 9-1-1, 9-2-2, 9-3-3, 9-4-4, 9-5-5, 9-6-6, 9-7-7, 9-8-8 — eight archetypes.

Group X-9-X (etheric field in the Zhi position; basic field X in the Ma and Kun positions): 1-9-1, 2-9-2, 3-9-3, 4-9-4, 5-9-5, 6-9-6, 7-9-7, 8-9-8 — eight archetypes.

Sum: 16 integral archetypes.

The principled distinguishing mark of the integral archetypes is the doubled reinforcement of a single basic field. In the code of an integral archetype, the field X is encountered twice (in Zhi and Kun, or in Ma and Kun). This means that the functional characteristic corresponding to the basic field is expressed within the personality with doubled intensity. To this doubling is added the presence of the etheric field (9), which is correlated within the Dar system with the integrative, unifying, wholistic principle.

The conjunction of two factors — the doubled reinforcement of the basic field and etheric integration — creates a unique psychological configuration not reducible to the combination of three distinct basic fields (as in the majority of basic archetypes).

6.2. The Psychological Function of the Integral

Psychologically, the integral archetype represents a type of personality in which the leading modality of the field X is developed and integrated to a greater degree than in any basic archetype of the same field. The bearer of an integral archetype of the field X encompasses the potential of the entire family of basic archetypes of the field X — that is, is capable of realising the functional possibilities of all seven basic archetypes possessing X in the Kun position.

For example, the integral archetype 1-9-1 (the LOGOS field in Ma and Kun, ether in Zhi) contains within its psychological function the potential of all seven basic archetypes of the LOGOS family: LA-DA (2-8-1), I-STOK (3-7-1), ZHAR (4-6-1), TE-LO (5-5-1), SVE-TO (6-4-1), PRI-TOK (7-3-1), LE-LI (8-2-1). This does not mean that the bearer of 1-9-1 simultaneously expresses all seven basic patterns; it means that the personality has an integrated access to all the modalities of the LOGOS field and is able to unfold the corresponding functions according to the situation.

In an analogous manner, the integral archetype 9-1-1 integrates the same potential of the LOGOS family, but with a different structural accentuation: ether in the Ma position (inner potential) with the doubled expression of LOGOS in Zhi (realisation) and Kun (synthesis). The difference between 9-X-X and X-9-X lies in the level at which etheric integration is manifested: at the level of the inner potential or at the level of the outer realisation.

Within the authorial tradition of the Dar system, the integral archetypes are regarded as a type of personality of heightened maturity and greater breadth of scope. According to the author’s observations over five years of practical work with the system, bearers of integral archetypes frequently exhibit the capacity to encompass multiple sides of a single situation, to act simultaneously in several functional registers, and to adapt their strategy to various contexts without losing substantive connection with the leading field. At the same time, bearers of integral archetypes may experience specific difficulties bound to the great breadth of scope: difficulty of specialisation, the risk of dispersal, the need for a longer period to find one’s own form of realisation.

The substantive descriptions of the integral archetypes have undergone repeated verification in the author’s practical work and in observations of bearers of these types; their description corresponds to the actual personal and behavioural patterns of bearers to the same degree as is observed for the basic archetypes.

6.3. The Relation of the Integral Archetype to the Basic Archetypes of the Same Field

The particular place of the integral archetype within the system requires an explicit description of its relation to the basic archetypes of the corresponding field. This relation has several facets.

The structural relation. All basic archetypes of the field X have the value X in the Kun position, and the integral archetypes of the field X have the value X in two positions (one of which is also Kun). Thus the integral archetype of the field X and the basic archetypes of the field X share a common point of synthesis — the field X. This creates a “family in the broader sense,” uniting the seven basic archetypes with the two integrals.

The functional relation. The psychological functions realised by the individual basic archetypes of the field X (the specialised patterns) are present within the bearer of the integral archetype of the same field as accessible modalities, activated according to the situation. Stated otherwise: the seven specialisations become the seven “options” of a single integral type.

The developmental relation. Within the authorial tradition of the Dar system, the possibility is considered that the bearer of a basic archetype of the field X may, in the course of life, “grow up to” the integral level of the same field — expanding the specialisation to the integrated scope of the whole field. This process is not automatic and is not guaranteed; it is bound up with conscious work upon oneself, with the expansion of psychological experience, with the assimilation into oneself of the various modalities of the same field. This aspect is addressed to a separate applied work and is not unfolded in detail within the present monograph.

The hierarchical relation. Structurally, the integral archetype occupies a “higher” position within the system in comparison with the basic archetypes of the same field — in the sense of greater breadth of scope. This does not make it “better” or “more developed” in an evaluative sense; it is a structural characterisation, attesting to the greater complexity of the personality’s configuration.

With these relations in view, the description of each integral archetype in the following section contains explicit references to the family of basic archetypes that it integrates.

6.4. A Systematic Exposition of the 16 Integral Archetypes

The present section presents descriptions of all 16 integral archetypes. The descriptions are grouped pairwise: for each basic field X, the archetype of the 9-X-X group is described first, then the archetype of the X-9-X group. The descriptions are set out according to a compact template analogous to those of the basic archetypes in Chapter 5, with an emphasis on the integral nature.

The names of the integral archetypes, in distinction from the basic, are at the time of writing of the present monograph not fixed within the authorial tradition (see § 6.5). Within the descriptions, the structural codes and scientific designations are employed; concrete “Dar names” analogous to the names of the basic archetypes (ZHAR, I-STOK, LU-NA, and others) will be elaborated in subsequent works.

Integral archetypes of the LOGOS field

9-1-1 — Integrator of the LOGOS Field (Type I)

Configuration: OMA — LOGOS — LOGOS. Etheric integration in the position of inner potential; the doubled expression of the structural principle in the positions of realisation and synthesis.

Sacred energy: an integral connection with the structural principle, manifesting outwardly as a strong organising function. The bearer leans upon intuitive wholeness and realises it through the doubled capacity for structuring.

Light side: a wide integral competence in the creation of structures; the capacity to see several levels of organisation simultaneously and to work with them in a single key. Those around perceive the bearer as a “universal structurer” capable of bringing order to any system.

Shadows. Active: the expansion of the structuring function into areas that have no need of it. Passive: the impossibility of finding a point of application for the integral competence. Deep fear: of the non-engagement of the integral potential.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the LOGOS family.

1-9-1 — Integrator of the LOGOS Field (Type II)

Configuration: LOGOS — OMA — LOGOS. The doubled expression of the structural principle in the positions of potential and synthesis; etheric integration in the position of realisation.

Sacred energy: an integral connection with the structural principle, manifesting through the etheric phase of realisation. The bearer leans upon a stable structural foundation and realises it through integrating, unifying action.

Light side: deep structural maturity with an integrating style of action; the capacity to create order not through forceful imposition but through the gradual binding of disparate elements. Those around perceive the bearer as a “harmonising structurer.”

Shadows. Active: a hypertrophy of the integrating function (the attempt to join the unjoinable). Passive: the dissolution of the structural principle within the etheric phase. Deep fear: of the loss of structural identity in the process of integration.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the LOGOS family, with a particular emphasis on the harmonising archetypes (LA-DA, TE-LO).

Integral archetypes of the NIMA field

9-2-2 — Integrator of the NIMA Field (Type I)

Configuration: OMA — NIMA — NIMA. Etheric integration in the potential; the doubled expression of the field of spaciousness in realisation and synthesis.

Sacred energy: wholeness manifesting through spaciousness; the capacity to encompass multiplicity as a single field of possibilities.

Light side: a wide consciousness with stability; the simultaneous holding of many variants without the loss of orientation. Those around perceive the bearer as a “person of many possibilities.”

Shadows. Active: a hypertrophy of spaciousness, dispersal. Passive: a paralysis of choice. Deep fear: of being limited.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the NIMA family.

2-9-2 — Integrator of the NIMA Field (Type II)

Configuration: NIMA — OMA — NIMA. The doubled expression of the field of spaciousness in potential and synthesis; etheric integration in realisation.

Sacred energy: an inner spaciousness realising itself through integrating action and returning to spaciousness in synthesis.

Light side: a deep inner multidimensionality manifesting through etheric-unifying action; the capacity to give spaciousness to others while simultaneously gathering all into a whole. In the bearer’s presence those around feel at once freedom and connectedness.

Shadows. Active: an intrusive integration of another’s spaciousness. Passive: the impossibility of realising one’s own spaciousness. Deep fear: that spaciousness will remain unrealised.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the NIMA family.

Integral archetypes of the ANDRA field

9-3-3 — Integrator of the ANDRA Field (Type I)

Configuration: OMA — ANDRA — ANDRA. Etheric integration in the potential; the doubled expression of the connective principle in realisation and synthesis.

Sacred energy: wholeness manifesting through connection; an integral sense of warmth and empathy directed outwards with doubled intensity.

Light side: a deep capacity to create and to sustain connections in the most diverse contexts simultaneously; an integral empathy embracing a wide field of relationships. Those around perceive the bearer as “the person who connects everyone.”

Shadows. Active: a hypertrophy of the connective function (the striving to join all to all). Passive: burnout from the volume of empathic labour. Deep fear: of the rupture of connectedness in its integral dimension.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the ANDRA family.

3-9-3 — Integrator of the ANDRA Field (Type II)

Configuration: ANDRA — OMA — ANDRA. The doubled expression of the connective principle in potential and synthesis; etheric integration in realisation.

Sacred energy: an inner warmth realising itself through integrating action and returning to connection in synthesis.

Light side: a deep inner warmth manifesting through etheric-unifying action; the capacity not merely to connect people but to integrate them into a common whole field.

Shadows. Active: the dissolution of self within a common “warm field.” Passive: the loss of one’s own empathic sensitivity. Deep fear: that one’s own connection has been an illusion.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the ANDRA family.

Integral archetypes of the ZINGRA field

9-4-4 — Integrator of the ZINGRA Field (Type I)

Configuration: OMA — ZINGRA — ZINGRA. Etheric integration in the potential; the doubled expression of the transformative principle in realisation and synthesis.

Sacred energy: wholeness manifesting through transformation; the integral capacity to initiate changes.

Light side: a wide competence in the field of transformations; the capacity to lead deep transformations with awareness of their influence upon the whole. Those around perceive the bearer as a “universal transformer.”

Shadows. Active: revolutionism for the sake of revolutionism. Passive: paralysis in the face of the magnitude of possible changes. Deep fear: of the cessation of the transformative process as a whole.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the ZINGRA family.

4-9-4 — Integrator of the ZINGRA Field (Type II)

Configuration: ZINGRA — OMA — ZINGRA. The doubled expression of the transformative principle in potential and synthesis; etheric integration in realisation.

Sacred energy: an inner fire realising itself through integrating action and returning to transformation in synthesis.

Light side: a deep inner drive towards development manifesting through etheric-unifying action; the capacity to lead transformations gently, without destroying what should be preserved.

Shadows. Active: an intrusive transformation of those around. Passive: the dimming of transformative force within the etheric phase. Deep fear: that the transformation has been out of place.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the ZINGRA family.

Integral archetypes of the LUBA field

9-5-5 — Integrator of the LUBA Field (Type I)

Configuration: OMA — LUBA — LUBA. Etheric integration in the potential; the doubled expression of the centring principle in realisation and synthesis.

Sacred energy: wholeness manifesting through centring; an integral “regal” pattern with doubled volitional intensity.

Light side: a deep inner centredness with wide scope; the capacity to be “the centre that sees all.” Those around perceive the bearer as a natural leader of integral level.

Shadows. Active: a hypertrophy of leadership, an expansion of the centre. Passive: the refusal of the central role in the presence of the capacity to occupy it. Deep fear: of the loss of the integral centre.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the LUBA family.

5-9-5 — Integrator of the LUBA Field (Type II)

Configuration: LUBA — OMA — LUBA. The doubled expression of the centring principle in potential and synthesis; etheric integration in realisation.

Sacred energy: an inner centre realising itself through integrating action and returning to the centre in synthesis.

Light side: a deep inner axis manifesting through etheric-unifying action; the capacity not only to hold the centre but to gather all around it.

Shadows. Active: the dissolution of the centre within the collective. Passive: the loss of one’s own centre in the striving to integrate all. Deep fear: that the centre has been fictitious.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the LUBA family.

Integral archetypes of the TUMA field

9-6-6 — Integrator of the TUMA Field (Type I)

Configuration: OMA — TUMA — TUMA. Etheric integration in the potential; the doubled expression of the field of movement in realisation and synthesis.

Sacred energy: wholeness manifesting through movement; an integral sense of rhythm encompassing various temporal scales simultaneously.

Light side: a deep sense of the flow with the simultaneous holding of different temporal scales; the capacity to lead long-lasting processes. Those around perceive the bearer as a “person of long breath.”

Shadows. Active: a hypertrophy of the sense of flow, a flight from stability. Passive: a freezing within one of the temporal scales. Deep fear: of the rupture of temporal wholeness.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the TUMA family.

6-9-6 — Integrator of the TUMA Field (Type II)

Configuration: TUMA — OMA — TUMA. The doubled expression of the field of movement in potential and synthesis; etheric integration in realisation.

Sacred energy: an inner rhythm realising itself through integrating action and returning to rhythm in synthesis.

Light side: a deep inner rhythm manifesting through etheric-unifying action; the capacity to hold one’s own rhythm and simultaneously to gather the various rhythms of those around into a common harmony.

Shadows. Active: the imposition of one’s own rhythm as the common. Passive: the loss of one’s own rhythm in the attempt to accommodate the common. Deep fear: that one’s own rhythm has no integral significance.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the TUMA family.

Integral archetypes of the ASTRA field

9-7-7 — Integrator of the ASTRA Field (Type I)

Configuration: OMA — ASTRA — ASTRA. Etheric integration in the potential; the doubled expression of the field of the word in realisation and synthesis.

Sacred energy: wholeness manifesting through the word; an integral communicative capacity with doubled verbal intensity.

Light side: a wide communicative competence; the capacity to find a common language with different people and at the same time to join them through speech. Those around perceive the bearer as a “universal communicator.”

Shadows. Active: a hypertrophy of speech-activity. Passive: the impossibility of finding a point of application for the communicative competence. Deep fear: of integral muteness.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the ASTRA family.

7-9-7 — Integrator of the ASTRA Field (Type II)

Configuration: ASTRA — OMA — ASTRA. The doubled expression of the field of the word in potential and synthesis; etheric integration in realisation.

Sacred energy: an inner word realising itself through integrating action and returning to the word in synthesis.

Light side: a deep inner speech manifesting through etheric-unifying action; the capacity not only to speak clearly but to join disparate meanings into a whole.

Shadows. Active: an intrusive joining of meanings. Passive: the loss of one’s own speech-position in the striving to join those of others. Deep fear: that the word does not reach the integral level.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the ASTRA family.

Integral archetypes of the BITRA field

9-8-8 — Integrator of the BITRA Field (Type I)

Configuration: OMA — BITRA — BITRA. Etheric integration in the potential; the doubled expression of the field of boundaries in realisation and synthesis.

Sacred energy: wholeness manifesting through form; the integral capacity to hold boundaries with doubled protective intensity.

Light side: a wide competence in the establishment of boundaries; the capacity to protect the multiple while preserving connectedness. Those around perceive the bearer as a “reliable keeper.”

Shadows. Active: a hypertrophy of the protective function, isolation. Passive: the loss of the capacity to hold boundaries in the face of the magnitude. Deep fear: of the disintegration of the integral form.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the BITRA family.

8-9-8 — Integrator of the BITRA Field (Type II)

Configuration: BITRA — OMA — BITRA. The doubled expression of the field of boundaries in potential and synthesis; etheric integration in realisation.

Sacred energy: an inner form realising itself through integrating action and returning to form in synthesis.

Light side: a deep inner contour manifesting through etheric-unifying action; the capacity not only to defend one’s own but to join disparate protected spaces into a common whole.

Shadows. Active: an intrusive joining of protected spaces. Passive: the loss of one’s own contour in the striving towards integration. Deep fear: that the boundary will be lost within the etheric phase.

Connection with the basic family: integrates all seven basic archetypes of the BITRA family.

6.5. The Open Task of Symbolic Nomination

In distinction from the 64 basic archetypes, each of which possesses a fixed name within the authorial tradition of the Dar system (LA-DA, I-STOK, ZHAR, TE-LO, SVE-TO, PRI-TOK, LE-LI for the LOGOS family, and analogously for the others), the 16 integral archetypes, at the time of writing of the present monograph, do not possess fixed names. This is a methodological choice on the part of the author, not a defect of the system.

Names within the authorial tradition are not arbitrary designations; they are the result of a long observational process within which a name “germinates” from the actual experience of interaction with bearers of the archetype. Since integral archetypes occur in the population less frequently than the basic (in view of the additional conditions on the configuration of the date of birth), the accumulation of an observational basis for them requires a longer period. The names of the integral archetypes will be formed by the authors gradually, in the course of continuing practical work with the system; their fixation within the authorial tradition is an open task, indicated as one of the directions of subsequent publications.

Within the present monograph, the following are employed for the integral archetypes:

structural codes (for example, 1-9-1, 9-3-3) — the principal technically precise designation;

scientific designations in the format “Integrator of the field X (Type I or II)” — for academic use.

This decision secures the correctness of scholarly usage while preserving the openness of the authorial process. The names will be added to the system at such time as they are formed by the authors with the same thoroughness with which the names of the basic archetypes were formed in their own time.

Concerning “Types I and II” (that is, the difference between the groups 9-X-X and X-9-X): within the authorial tradition, they are distinguished by substantive directedness (Type I — etheric integration in the position of potential; Type II — etheric integration in the position of realisation). These differences require a separate research elaboration, which also belongs to the programme of future works.

In the present chapter, the 16 integral archetypes of the Dar system have been systematically described — a separate class of archetypes differing from the basic both structurally (the doubled reinforcement of a single basic field plus an etheric component) and psychologically (the integral function embracing all the basic archetypes of the corresponding field).

The structural particularities of the integral class (the formula 9-X-X / X-9-X), its psychological function, and its relation to the basic archetypes of the same field have been described, together with each of the 16 integral archetypes in its individual exposition.

The open task of the symbolic nomination of the integral archetypes has been indicated as a direction of future research.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. The Special Archetype 9-9-9
chapters.html:
The third and last class of archetypes within the Dar model contains a single archetype — the configuration 9-9-9, in which all three positions of the triadic structure (Ma, Zhi, Kun) are occupied by the etheric field OMA (numerical code 9). This is a unique case: none of the 64 basic and none of the 16 integral archetypes reproduces this configuration. The archetype 9-9-9 stands apart within the system, occupying its own ontological position.

The present chapter is devoted to the description of its structural particularity (§ 7.1), its psychological nature (§ 7.2), its typological status in comparison with the archetype of the Self in the tradition of C. G. Jung (§ 7.3), its empirical rarity and the observational situation (§ 7.4), and the open field of research tasks that the 9-9-9 archetype presents to the author and to the scholarly community (§ 7.5).

The description of the 9-9-9 archetype in the present chapter is deliberately more unfolded than the description of an individual basic or integral archetype. This is bound up with the fact that it constitutes a subtle object demanding careful conceptual work, and at the same time with the fact that its empirical rarity renders each observation particularly valuable.

7.1. Structural Particularity

The 9-9-9 archetype is formed on the condition that the digital root of all three positions of the triadic code — Ma, Zhi, and Kun, computed from the date of birth according to the algorithm of Chapter 4 — equals 9. That is:

Ma position = dr(day + month) = 9 → the etheric field OMA (potential expression);

Zhi position = dr(year) = 9 → the etheric field OMA (actual expression);

Kun position = dr(Ma + Zhi) = dr(9 + 9) = dr(18) = 9 → the etheric field OMA (synthesising expression).

All three positions are closed upon one and the same field — the etheric field OMA, which within the Dar model occupies a particular position. In distinction from the eight basic fields (LOGOS, NIMA, ANDRA, ZINGRA, LUBA, TUMA, ASTRA, BITRA), each of which is responsible for a specific energetic register, the field OMA has no specialisation of its own. It corresponds to the integrative, support-free, universal register — the space within which all the remaining fields dwell as pure possibility.

From Chapter 6 it is known that the 16 integral archetypes also contain the field OMA in one of their positions (Ma or Zhi), and it is this that renders them integral — that is, containing in folded form all the basic archetypes of the corresponding field. Within each integral archetype, however, there is also a second field — a basic one (LOGOS, NIMA, …, BITRA) — which gives the thematic directedness of the integration. Thus the integral archetype 9-1-1 / 1-9-1 integrates all the archetypes of the LOGOS field, the archetype 9-2-2 / 2-9-2 — all the archetypes of the NIMA field, and so forth.

The archetype 9-9-9 differs from the integrals in that it possesses no second field. All three positions are occupied by OMA, and thematic specialisation is entirely absent. This is integration without specialisation — a state in which all basic fields are contained simultaneously as pure potentiality, with no one of them set apart.

If one represents the complete topology of the 81 archetypes as a three-dimensional space, along each of whose axes are arranged 9 values (the 9 basic fields), then:

the 64 basic archetypes occupy the “edge” region of the space (without the participation of the etheric field OMA in the Ma and Zhi positions);

the 16 integral archetypes occupy a “face” of the space (where OMA participates in one of the first two positions);

the archetype 9-9-9 occupies the single “apex” point — the point at which all three coordinates equal 9.

This apex point is the centre of symmetry of the entire space of the model. The other 80 archetypes arrange themselves around it in a precisely described geometric configuration: each basic archetype has its “mirror,” each field has its pair of integral archetypes, and only the archetype 9-9-9 has no inner pair. It is alone.

7.2. Psychological Nature

Psychologically, the archetype 9-9-9 is described through the category of pure integrativity — a condition in which all potentials, all modes of expression, all archetypal themes are contained simultaneously, yet none of them is set apart as dominant.

The bearer of the archetype 9-9-9 has no specialisation in the ordinary typological sense. He or she is not a “leader,” not a “communicator,” not a “creator,” not a “guardian” — but contains all these modes in folded form, and any of them may be actualised at the needed moment. This property creates a characteristic picture: outwardly such a person is perceived as “one without a clearly expressed type,” “universal,” “fluid,” “many-faced.”

Yet such universality is given not as an easy openness but as a heavy task of integration. The bearer of the archetype 9-9-9 must learn to work consciously with any of the eight basic fields at the needed moment, without permitting any of them to seize him or her wholly. This requires a high level of inner differentiation — paradoxically, to be integral, one must learn to differentiate.

In the authors’ practice, stable phenomenological features typical of the bearers of the archetype 9-9-9 have been recorded (with the reservation that the observational base is small and each case requires individual verification):

the absence of an unambiguous answer to the question “Who am I?” — the bearer does not find himself or herself within any of the standard typological classifications;

the capacity for deep contact with any type of interlocutor — the phenomenon of “mimicry without loss of self”;

the experience of invisibility — the feeling that those around do not see them as “real,” because there is no fixed form for recognition;

an attraction to integrative practices — meditation, philosophy, psychotherapy, mystical experience, systems thinking;

a late social self-identification — bearers of the archetype 9-9-9 frequently attain a stable sense of self significantly later than their peers;

a heightened sensitivity to collective conditions — the capacity to read the emotional field of a group as a wholeness.

The deep fear of the bearer of the archetype 9-9-9 is the fear of dissolving without remainder, of losing one’s own form upon contact with any strong external influence. Since he or she has no single dominant field that could serve as a “protective shell,” the openness is experienced as vulnerability.

This is no neurotic symptom. It is a structural feature of the archetype itself. Working with it presupposes not “deliverance,” but the development of the capacity to hold the centre under conditions of principled indeterminacy — a task akin to the mature spiritual practices.

The motto formulated by the author as a generalisation of the psychological content of the archetype:

“I am the point at which all possibilities meet.”

7.3. Typological Status in Comparison with the Jungian Self

The archetype of the Self (Ger. das Selbst; Eng. the Self) occupies a central place within the analytical psychology of C. G. Jung. The Self is described by Jung as:

the centre and at the same time the whole wholeness of the psyche;

the archetype uniting the conscious and the unconscious;

the organising principle towards which the process of individuation strives;

symbolically expressed in the mandala — the concentric structure with a centre and an encompassing periphery.

Between the archetype of the Self and the archetype 9-9-9 in the authorial Dar system there is to be found a number of structural parallels:

Both occupy a central position within their typological topology. In Jung — the centre of the psyche; in the Dar model — the central point of the space of 81 archetypes.

Both possess an integrative function. The Self unites the opposites; the archetype 9-9-9 contains within itself all the basic fields simultaneously.

Both are described through the category of wholeness rather than through specialisation.

Both are bound up with late development. Individuation in Jung unfolds in the second half of life; bearers of 9-9-9 typically attain a stable identity later than their peers.

In both traditions, the corresponding archetypes are rarely experienced directly — more often as a direction of development, as a horizon of work.

Between the two categories there are also substantive differences that exclude direct identification:

Universality vs. individuality. The archetype of the Self in Jung’s conception is inherent in every person — it is a structural element of any psyche. The archetype 9-9-9 in the Dar model is an individual typological characteristic actualised only under a definite biographical configuration (approximately 1% of the population; see § 7.4).

Metaphysical vs. algorithmic status. The Self in Jung is formulated in the metaphysical categories of the collective unconscious; the archetype 9-9-9 in the Dar model is defined deterministically by biographical parameters.

Goal vs. givenness. The Self is that towards which the process of individuation moves; the archetype 9-9-9 is that with which the bearer is already born, and which becomes for him or her both a point of support and a psychological task simultaneously.

We compare 9-9-9 with the Jungian Self not in order to identify the two, but as a heuristic. The comparison permits:

giving the bearer of the archetype 9-9-9 a language for the description of his or her own experience, leaning upon the elaborated Jungian tradition;

including the authorial Dar model within the wider context of the depth psychology of the twentieth–twenty-first centuries;

delineating a psychotherapeutic perspective for work with bearers of the archetype (through the known practices of work with the Self — active imagination, amplification, work with dreams).

7.4. Empirical Rarity and the Observational Situation

Of the 81 equiprobable (under uniform distribution) configurations, only one corresponds to the archetype 9-9-9. This gives a theoretical frequency of approximately 1.23% (1/81) under the assumption of full independence and uniformity of the distribution of digital roots of date of birth.

In actual distributions, the frequency may differ from the theoretical. The digital roots of dates of birth are not perfectly uniform: the distribution depends upon the particularities of the calendar and the time of the fixation of births within the population. This question requires a separate empirical investigation.

In the authors’ pilot observations (the practice of computation from 2021 to 2026, more than 3,000 computations), the frequency of the archetype 9-9-9 amounted to approximately 0.8–1.0% of the general sample. This is consistent with the theoretical value.

The small number of bearers of the archetype 9-9-9 creates a particular research situation. On the one hand, each recorded case represents valuable material. On the other, generalisations require caution, since a small sample does not permit a strict separation of the structural particularities of the archetype from individual biographical factors.

Within the programme of further research (see Chapter 10), a targeted expansion of the sample of bearers of the archetype 9-9-9 is envisaged through an announcement on the research platform nauka-yupdar.vercel.app of a special invitation protocol for users with this configuration.

7.5. The Open Field of Research Tasks

The archetype 9-9-9 presents to the author and to the scholarly community several research tasks, only partially resolved within the present monograph:

Task 1. The expansion of the observational base. A targeted collection of data on bearers of the archetype 9-9-9 with detailed biographical and psychological dimensions (within protocols agreed with an ethics committee).

Task 2. Empirical verification of the phenomenological features. Verification of the particularities enumerated in § 7.2 on a statistically significant sample, with the use of standardised psychological techniques (tests of typological indeterminacy, the measurement of late self-identification, scales of empathy and sensitivity).

Task 3. Comparison with other typological “central” categories. In addition to Jung’s Self — the archetype of the Perfect Human (Insān al-Kāmil) in the Sufi tradition; the conception of a universal type within the Enneagram (if such an interpretation is possible); the category of the rhizome in Deleuze and Guattari. This is material for a separate philosophical-methodological work.

Task 4. A psychotherapeutic protocol. The elaboration of a particular protocol of work with bearers of the archetype 9-9-9, taking into account the structural openness and the basic fear of dissolution. This task belongs to an applied monograph on the use of the Dar model in psycho-emotional self-regulation and does not enter into the bounds of the present work.

Task 5. Symbolic nomination. The archetype 9-9-9, like the integral archetypes, at present possesses within the authorial tradition no fixed symbolic name of its own. The search for such a name — reflecting simultaneously the central position and the universal character of the archetype — remains an open research task.

In the present chapter, a description has been presented of the special archetype 9-9-9 — the sole representative of the third class of archetypes within the authorial Dar system. Structurally, this archetype is defined by the configuration in which all three positions of the triadic structure are occupied by the etheric field OMA (9-9-9). Psychologically, it is described through the category of pure integrativity — a condition in which all basic fields are contained simultaneously as potentiality without specialisation. The basic fear is dissolution without remainder; the task of development is to learn to hold the centre under conditions of principled indeterminacy. The archetype is compared with the archetype of the Self in the tradition of C. G. Jung by structural parallels (central position, integrative function, connection with late development), but is not identified with it. The empirical frequency amounts to approximately 1% of the population and is confirmed by the author’s pilot observations. The archetype poses a number of research tasks, partially formulated in the present chapter and continuing the programme of future work (see Chapter 10).

References

chapters.title: Chapter 8. The YupLand Digital Ecosystem as an Artifact of Embodiment
chapters.html:
The present chapter describes the YupLand digital ecosystem as an artifact of embodiment of the noumenal structure of the Dar model. The concept of embodiment, introduced in Chapter 2 within the philosophical-methodological section, here acquires concrete technological and architectural content.

YupLand is a decentralised Web3 ecosystem (a metaverse) built around the Dar typological model as its architectural core. Each user’s individual archetype is computed algorithmically and shapes that user’s personal path within the ecosystem. The noumenal construction (the declared typology) thereby acquires an observable incarnation within the digital environment, whose phenomena are accessible to empirical investigation (Chapter 9).

The chapter unfolds, in sequence: the history, self-definition, and ideological principles of the project; the cultural code and the figure of Yupik as the digital double of the user; the architecture of the ecosystem — social (a two-level structure: four classes of participants and ten scale-generations), technological, and product-related; the YupDar application as the point of entry into the system; the Principle of Dar-Giving, the cryptocurrency DarAi with its distribution structure, the NFT-reputation system, and the contour of ethical artificial intelligence; the modes of embodiment of the typology within the product contours; the methodological consequences of the consideration of YupLand as an object of scholarly observation; and the evolutionary stages of the ecosystem’s development.

8.1. The History and Ideology of the Project

YupLand arose as a joint initiative of Ya. S. Sibirskiy, S. N. Nesterova, and other Architects of the system in the early 2020s. The ecosystem grew from a practical need: to make the Dar system accessible to a wider audience in a form that goes beyond either the printed book or the one-to-one consultation. The digital environment made it possible to combine the algorithmic precision of computation (the deterministic nature of the profile) with an interactive experience (the user’s possibility “to live” within his or her archetype).

Ya. S. Sibirskiy has acted as co-founder of the ecosystem, bearer of the conceptual core of the Dar system, and game designer. S. N. Nesterova — co-founder, architect of the educational direction, developer of the YupDar application (from conception to programmatic implementation), and author of The Book of DARs (2026), which has served as the substantive foundation of the educational contour of the ecosystem. Within the ecosystem other DevOps projects are also realised on the NEAR blockchain platform.

The authors of the ecosystem define YupLand as a hybrid intellectual noosphere — a space within which technological, cognitive, and spiritual practices converge into a single environment of joint development. Within this formula three words are key:

Hybrid — indicates the conscious joining of different registers ordinarily kept separate (science and spirituality, economy and ethics, individual and collective development);

Intellectual — indicates the role of the educational and research contour as the core of the ecosystem;

Noosphere — indicates the digital nature of the space as a sphere of mind, while not reducing it to the entertainment metaverse of mass culture.

In the project’s presentation materials, YupLand is defined as “a living ecosystem in which technology and spirituality, science and finance merge into a single flow,” and as “a game in which progress is preserved not on the computer but in the user’s actual actions — in learning, co-creation, helping people.” These formulations fix the central methodological orientation of the project: the inner progress of the user is not a game-abstraction but the reflection of actual transformations within his or her everyday life.

The YupLand ecosystem is built upon several principles that distinguish it from standard commercial metaverses:

The Teal model of organisation. The management of the ecosystem is structured according to principles known in contemporary management theory as “Teal” (F. Laloux): self-management, wholeness, and conscious evolution. This means the absence of a rigid hierarchical verticality, the transparency of decision-making, and the priority of the inner motivation of participants over external control.

The Principle of Dar-Giving as the organisational foundation. The basic model of interaction within the ecosystem is the exchange of Dars, not the transaction. The cryptocurrency DarAi (see § 8.4) technically realises this principle at the level of the internal economy.

Educational priority. The entertainment and social contours of the ecosystem are subordinated to the task of the user’s acquaintance with his or her archetype and the development of practices of working with Dars through the nurturing of the Yupik avatar.

An open community of practitioners. YupLand is not constructed as a closed consumer space; users are invited to co-creation, investigation, and the exchange of experience.

Respect for the original source. The ecosystem consistently acknowledges the authorship of Ya. S. Sibirskiy as the founder of the Dar system; a part of the revenues is directed back into the development of the ecosystem (see § 8.4).

The collective nature of knowledge. Within the project’s materials the metaphor of hive mind is emphasised — the collective intelligence forming itself out of the living communication of participants and engendering “real-time datasets.” This metaphor reflects the orientation towards the construction of knowledge not as an individual product but as the result of the coordinated work of the community. The ecosystem investigates the motivational stimuli and behavioural patterns of participants, transforming them into game-mechanics.

For the securing of the connectedness and recognisability of the ecosystem, the authors of the project formulate a four-axis cultural code — the set of basic orientations shared by participants of the community:

Awareness — the capacity to recognise one’s own emotions and motives, and to see the influence of one’s actions upon those around.

Curiosity — the readiness to investigate the new, to test hypotheses, to pose uncomfortable questions.

Honesty — the quality of interactions, the transparency of intentions, the fulfilment of promises, sincerity.

Strength — the responsible disposition of one’s own resources (time, attention, material means, symbolic capital).

These four categories function not as a formal code but as a frame of mutual recognition within the community. They are neutral with respect to concrete spiritual or worldview systems, religions, nationalities, languages of communication — which permits the ecosystem to accommodate participants of various origins without dilution of its own identity. The community of the ecosystem at present comprises more than 150,000 participants from 25 countries of the world.

Yupik: The Digital Double of the User

At the symbolic heart of the ecosystem stands the figure of Yupik — the avatar-character representing the user within the digital space. The authorial conception defines Yupik not as a game-avatar in the ordinary sense but as a digital double, whose characteristics and development are bound to the user’s actual actions within the physical world. The name “Yupik” goes back to a root with the meaning living.

The development of Yupik takes place along three axes: growth through actions (when the user learns, creates, gives); transformation through challenges (when the user encounters difficulties and overcomes them); and recognition through the individual archetype (when Yupik visually and behaviourally reflects the Dar of its bearer). Yupik thereby becomes the symbolic embodiment of the four-axis cultural code in individual form.

Within the framework of the present investigation, the scholarly part of the ecosystem is represented by a separate research platform accessible at the address nauka-yupdar.vercel.app. This platform is intended for the collection of empirical data concerning the self-recognition of users in the personal archetype, and is described in Chapter 9.

8.2. The Architecture of the Ecosystem

In addition to the technological infrastructure (see below), YupLand possesses an elaborated social architecture — a formal distribution of the roles of participants, reflecting the level of their contribution to the development of the ecosystem. The social architecture is realised at two levels: a coarse-grained level (four classes) and a fine-grained level (ten scale-generations of Yupiks).

The coarse-grained level: four classes of participants

Architects — the bearers of conceptual vision and strategy, responsible for the development of the model as a whole and for the adoption of key decisions concerning the direction of the ecosystem’s evolution.

Builders — participants who lead concrete product, research, and educational directions; developers, coordinators, authors of products, courses, and publications.

Residents — the principal mass of active users, mastering the educational programmes, participating in social interactions, and forming the living tissue of the community.

Collectors — participants who invest in the economic and cultural capital of the ecosystem through the acquisition of its values (NFT-kingdoms, tokens, artifacts), supporting the project financially and symbolically.

This four-class structure is realised not only ideologically but also technically, through the system of NFT-reputation and role-differentiation within the digital interfaces. The system of NFT-reputation management is one of the principal instruments of attention-management among participants and its fixation within reputational tokens; many of the game-mechanics employed in the ecosystem are connected with the acquisition, accumulation, resetting, and exchange of NFT-tokens containing reputational scores. Reputation may be positive or negative, depending on the conditions of the gamification.

In a playful form, people track those patterns of their behaviour that they have in actual life, as if through the prism of a magnifying glass: they attend to how they react in the game to certain losses and gains, how strongly they engage emotionally, how they relate generally to one or another situation, how they make decisions. The game is intended to act as a kind of “inoculation” for the user’s actual life: so that when a difficult situation arises in the present, the user acts more consciously and meaningfully, and does not fall into depressive or over-euphoric states.

The game of reputation is one of the principal element-instruments through which the learning of awareness and responsibility takes place — a learning imperceptible to newcomers and obvious to long-standing residents. Each participant may move between classes in measure with the development of his or her contribution and the realisation of personal and collective potential. The structure recalls classical models of social organisation rethought in digital form: the Architects fulfil the role of keepers of meanings, the Builders — of doers, the Residents — of the main collective wholeness, the Collectors — of supporting capital.

The fine-grained level: ten scale-generations

Within the coarse-grained structure, YupLand introduces a more subtle articulation of participants into ten generations of the Yupik scale. Each generation has its own number, intensity of participation in collective processes, and functional purpose within the ecosystem.

Mathematical regularity

The numerosity of the generations follows a clear geometric regularity: each succeeding generation contains twice as many representatives as the preceding (with a slight correction for the zeroth and the exclusive classes). Thus there arises a structure in which the aggregate numerosity of Residents (generations 5–9) is a multiple of the aggregate of Builders (generations 1–4), which in turn is a multiple of the Architects (generation 0). This proportion reflects the basic principle of a stable social organisation: a small number of bearers of meaning, an intermediate stratum of realisers, a wide base of everyday participants.

In parallel with numerosity, the individual “intensity of participation” in collective processes decreases in inverse proportion: from 100% for the Ancients to approximately 0.2% for the Commons. This inverse dependency (the more numerous the generation, the smaller the individual weight of each member) secures the balance between breadth of reach and depth of responsibility — a task that contemporary distributed communities solve with varying degrees of success.

A particular position is occupied by the 64 Exclusive Yupiks composing the DAO YUPLAND. Their number coincides with the number of basic archetypes within the Dar model (see Chapter 5) — a conscious architectural correspondence underscoring the link of the social organisation of the ecosystem with its typological core.

The functional contours of YupLand

The YupLand ecosystem contains several interconnected functional contours:

The contour of computation — realises the algorithm for the generation of the individual profile (see Chapter 4). It receives as input the user’s biographical parameters and returns the triadic code of the archetype.

The contour of description — provides the user with an unfolded description of his or her personal archetype (the Dar). It is realised in the form of an interactive interface with navigation by sections (Description of the Dar, Strength/Weakness, Motto, Meanings, Messages, and others).

The contour of learning — the educational module within which the user is acquainted with the theoretical foundations of the Dar system, as well as with the practices of work with his or her own archetype.

The contour of AI-messages — the embedded language module that forms a personalised message for the user on the basis of the archetype.

The contour of play — the gaming direction, oriented towards the mastering of archetypal roles through gamified scenarios.

The contour of community — the social layer that permits users to communicate, to exchange experience, to participate in joint events.

The economic contour — the internal cryptocurrency DarAi and the Principle of Dar-Giving (see § 8.4).

Technological foundation

The ecosystem is built upon contemporary Web3 technologies with the use of cloud infrastructure. The key technological choices are:

Frontend: Telegram Mini App + a web interface on standard JS frameworks, securing cross-platform access without the need for separate mobile applications;

Backend: serverless architecture on the Vercel platform, securing horizontal scalability;

Database: Supabase (on a PostgreSQL basis) — for the storage of user profiles, computations, and the history of interaction;

Language module: integration with contemporary language models (DeepSeek, Groq) with a fallback system securing the stability of operation should the principal provider become unavailable;

Web3 component: the development of a proprietary cryptocurrency DarAi on a compatible blockchain infrastructure (NEAR Protocol and TON).

The architectural choice of Telegram Mini App is determined by the task of minimising the barrier of entry — the user does not need to install a separate application but obtains access to the ecosystem through a familiar messenger. The active Russian-speaking community of the project uses Telegram as the principal space of communication, which renders the choice of Mini App natural.

Companion products of the ecosystem

In addition to the central application YupDar (see § 8.3), within YupLand there develops a family of companion products, each of which addresses its own task and at the same time strengthens the connectedness of the ecosystem:

Yupalka — the game entry into the ecosystem with a realised referral mechanic of “living referrals” (mutual care between the inviter and the invited). The product underwent incubation within the ecosystem and was distinguished as a winner at a profile hackathon.

The Alchemist’s Shop (Lavka Alkhimika) — an in-ecosystem product for the joint crafting of NFTs from various projects and blockchains; it realises cross-chain compatibility (NEAR + TON) and distributes a part of the transaction commissions to the project’s investors in the form of the DarAi token.

SENDER — a platform for the management of reputation, for trading, for interaction with an audience, and for the launch of game-mechanics; it supports both key blockchains and provides the technological infrastructure for the integration of external Web3 projects into the ecosystem.

These and other products of the ecosystem not mentioned within the present work create what is termed in the project materials sub-ecosystems — internal clusters of activity, each of which serves users of a definite type of interest.

One of the key architectural principles of the ecosystem is the permanence of user data. After the first computation, the user’s individual profile is preserved on the server (in the Supabase database) and is restored from there at each subsequent session. The browser’s local storage is used as a cache, not as a source of truth. This decision is dictated not by technical requirements but by the principle of respect for individual typological identity: once computed, the user’s archetype is his or her permanent characteristic and ought not to “fall away” because of technical circumstances.

8.3. The YupDar Application as the Point of Entry into the System

The YupDar application is a mobile-and-web application realising the principal user contours of YupLand. It is one of the points of entry into the ecosystem; through YupDar the user:

computes his or her personal archetype (the Dar);

receives an unfolded description of the archetype (characteristics, strengths and shadow aspects, motto, meanings, messages, meditations);

becomes acquainted with the basic theory of the Dar system;

receives a personalised AI-message;

interacts with other users through the referral mechanism;

obtains access to extended functions through the system of internal currency.

The substantive core of the application is an encyclopaedia of the 64 basic archetypes, describing each archetype according to a structure of 9 sections (name of the Dar and of the archetype, brief description, strengths, shadow expressions, motto, meanings, keys to the self, traps, mission, and others). The source of the content is the authorial materials of S. N. Nesterova, going back to the pedagogical tradition of Ya. S. Sibirskiy and fixed in The Book of DARs (2026).

The substantive core for the integral archetypes and for the archetype 9-9-9 is at present realised within YupDar in the form of separate descriptive modules, whose development continues in parallel with the deepening of the theoretical base.

Particular attention within the architecture of YupDar is given to the AI-message language module, which forms a personal address to the user on the basis of the archetype. The prompt of this module is constructed upon the principle of strict reliance upon the user’s concrete Dar: the message does not imitate a general “wise” text, but rests strictly upon the content of the nine fields of the archetype, upon the matrix of fields, and upon the structure of the Ma–Zhi–Kun triad. This technological decision is methodologically bound up with the philosophical orientation of the work: the digital artifact must remain faithful to the noumenal structure, not substituting for it a convenient typological imitation.

In the elaboration of the prompts, the author consistently fixes and blocks the language models’ tendency towards stylistic drift, the use of clichés, address to the reader in the third person, the use of terms of the model outside their proper place, and excessive poeticisation at the expense of semantic precision. Each updating of the prompt passes through a cycle of testing and harmonisation with the reference authorial style.

8.4. The Principle of Dar-Giving and the Cryptocurrency DarAi

At the foundation of the economic organisation of YupLand lies the Principle of Dar-Giving — the norm according to which the primary form of exchange within the ecosystem is the transfer of value from one participant to another without the expectation of an immediate equivalent return. This principle does not abolish commercial transactions (they too remain possible), but it determines the primary register of relationships.

The Principle of Dar-Giving has three sources:

The conceptual. Within the Dar system, each archetype is a gift — a potential transmitted to the person and realised through his or her life. The logic of giving is extrapolated from the level of the archetype to the level of social interactions within the ecosystem.

The ethical. The Principle of Dar-Giving stands opposed to the purely consumer model of metaverses, within which the user is regarded as a source of monetisation.

The pragmatic. Within communities of Dar practitioners, giving naturally arises as the means of sharing discoveries, experiences, and support; the ecosystem technically anchors a practice already established in fact.

DarAi is the proprietary cryptocurrency of the YupLand ecosystem, technically realising the Principle of Dar-Giving. The particularities of DarAi:

it functions as the internal unit of account within the product contours of YupLand;

it is distributed not only for financial transactions but also for participation in the ecosystem (the invitation of friends, activity within the community, co-creation);

it secures the transparency of giving-flows upon the blockchain;

it is realised upon the NEAR Protocol blockchain;

it has related product tokens (for example, Duplo on the TON blockchain) composing a distributed internal economy of the ecosystem;

in the long term it is oriented towards integration with external blockchain systems, which will permit participants of the ecosystem to receive a material measurement of their contribution.
